Preface
Millions of people worldwide who experience mental health conditions do not have access to effective care. Self-help can help increase access to care in all countries. By providing structured psychological techniques that people can use in their own time, these interventions can empower individuals to manage stress and improve their mental health.
Evidence shows that self-help interventions are effective, particularly for depression and anxiety, and these interventions are recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). These interventions are likely to play a key role in expanding access to evidence-based mental health care in numerous countries. Because they can be delivered in person or remotely, with limited support from trained non-specialists, they have the potential to reach large numbers of people across diverse settings.
This manual is designed to support decision-makers and practitioners in planning and implementing both unguided and guided self-help. It includes information on two WHO-developed programmes - Step-by-Step and Doing What Matters in Times of Stress - which are delivered individually, both of which have been rigorously tested in randomized controlled trials (RCTs. Typically, these programmes are offered with brief weekly remote support (around 15 minutes of time) from a trained helper, though different models of delivery are also possible, such as no support or face-to-face support.
Step-by-Step and Doing What Matters in Times of Stress have already been integrated into national services: both interventions have been scaled up nationwide in Thailand and Step-by-Step is available across Lebanon. These experiences, alongside strong research evidence, demonstrate the powerful contribution that self-help interventions can make to any mental health system. They offer a practical and effective way to bring care to more people, wherever they live.
Dr Jeremy Farrar Assistant Director-General Division of Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care

1. Introduction
Psychological self-help interventions 1 are a valuable addition to mental health services in countries of all income levels, especially to help scale up care for common mental health conditions. They are recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) to support people, or carers of people, experiencing a number of mental health, brain health and substance use conditions (1). 2 Some guided self-help interventions delivered individually (for example, for depression and anxiety) demonstrate a similar level of effectiveness as more intensive interventions (2, 3). A key benefit is that they can increase access to evidence-based support for large numbers of people.
Psychological self-help interventions provide exercises and techniques that a person can use to help manage psychological distress and symptoms of mental health and other conditions. They can be delivered through different media (such as mobile application, website, book, video or audio recording), individually or in groups. They are structured so that a person can work through them completely on their own (unguided) or with the addition of some support, such as a brief introduction and follow-ups from a health professional or weekly contact (for example, via email, instant message, telephone, video or in person) from a trained and supervised nonspecialist (guided). 3
Psychological self-help interventions require less provider time to deliver than many mental health interventions, which may reduce costs and increase access. Digital versions can be delivered across a whole country or geographical region. This feature of digital interventions may be critical in areas where access to supervision and training is limited, as helpers and supervisors can be centralized in a few locations with the intervention provided remotely to a population. Unguided self-help is cheaper and easier to implement, but it may have a smaller impact on improving mental health than guided self-help. Guided self-help may have increased effects, especially for people with more severe problems. Self-help interventions can be integrated into existing mental health services and can complement any other type of care.

1.1.1 Scope
This manual provides information to support decision-makers and workers in planning and implementing individually delivered, evidence-based, psychological self-help interventions. It describes the added value of these interventions and considers how, where and when they can be of most use. Other forms of self-help, such as self-help groups organized by people experiencing similar problems, or WHO's Self-Help Plus (SH+) intervention (4), are not explicitly covered, yet much of Chapter 1 is relevant for all evidence-based self-help interventions.
1 In this document we use the term "self-help intervention" or "self-help" to mean "psychological self-help intervention".
2 The terms "mental health symptoms" and "mental health conditions" are used in this manual, yet all information is relevant for the wider set of mental health, brain health and substance conditions.
3 In this document we use the term "helper" to refer to someone providing support with self-help interventions.
The manual is primarily based on evidence from research trials conducted by WHO with adults with common mental health conditions, but much of the information may be relevant for other conditions where there are similar evidence-based interventions, such as iSupport for carers of people with dementia and the web-based programme Alcohol E-health (5, 6), or for adolescents and youths where similar self-help interventions are also shown to be effective (7, 8).

1.1.1 Scope
This manual also provides detailed information on implementing two individually delivered, WHO psychological self-help interventions: Step-by-Step (SbS) (SbS content can be found in the Web Annex to this manual) and Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM) (9), which have been shown to be effective in several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (see Table 2.1 Overview of SbS and DWM for more information on the trials). Both can be provided unguided: as part of routine care, where the intervention is provided by primary health care staff with minimal support; or using a guided self-help model developed and tested by WHO and scaled up nationally in Lebanon and Thailand. In this model, people completing the self-help intervention receive brief support (15 minutes per week) from a trained non-specialist helper (typically a lay community provider), either by telephone or message (10, 11).
This model (including example scripts and templates) can be adapted for use with other evidencebased individually delivered self-help interventions.

1.1.2 Audience and structure
This manual is written for:
- programme managers in organizations who want to implement a self-help intervention; and
- the helpers, supervisors and other workers who will be involved in its delivery.
The document is divided into four main parts, including the annexes (Figure 1.1 Content overview of this document). These are as follows: relevant information giving a general introduction to selfhelp interventions (Chapter 1. Introduction); practical information for setting up and providing individually delivered self-help interventions, which covers both guided and unguided interventions broadly (Chapter 2. For organizations: how to set up individually delivered self-help) and provides specific information that is used in running guided self-help interventions (Chapter 3. Introduction to providing support in guided self-help and Chapter 4. How to provide support to service users); information specific to setting up SbS and DWM (Chapter 5. Information for helpers delivering Step-by-Step and Chapter 6. Information for helpers delivering Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM)); and annexes with scripts and other key tools for helpers.
If you are interested in setting up DWM or SbS as a guided intervention and want to know specifically how helpers deliver support in 15 minutes, you may want to start by reviewing Chapter 4. How to provide support to service users and then come back to the rest of the manual.

1.1.3 Approach to development
This document manual builds upon prior work involving testing and implementing the WHO psychological interventions Step-by-Step and Doing What Matters in Times of Stress. It originated from the need to develop resources for stakeholders to support implementation of WHO recommendations of self-help interventions for common mental health conditions. The development of both interventions and this manual was informed by an extensive literature review and consultation with experts. The process included focus group discussions, adaptation workshops, review of content by people with lived experience of mental health conditions, formative research and RCTs.
The guided self-help model presented in this manual has been rigorously tested through pilot trials, feasibility RCTs and definitive RCTs. The content draws from unpublished implementation manuals used in the various research trials. These findings have been updated to reflect further insights gained from WHO recommendations and from practical experience with delivering the interventions.
The Step-by-Step intervention material, included as web annex, was developed through an iterative process. Following an extensive literature review and expert consultations, an initial draft was created and subsequently reviewed by both experts and service users. Based on their feedback, revisions were made, and a first version of the intervention was piloted in Lebanon. Insights and feedback from this pilot and all other research phases were then incorporated into the final materials.

1.2.1 What is self-help?
Self-help is a diverse category of approaches whereby people use information to help themselves, with limited or no support from professionals or other helpers. This includes individually accessed self-help books or mobile applications, attending psychoeducation groups, mutual self-help groups run by peers experiencing similar problems, and other diverse approaches. This manual focuses on individual, evidence-based, psychological self-help interventions.
These self-help interventions:
- provide information, psychological exercises and techniques (such as slow breathing) that a person learns and completes in their own time to help manage stress and symptoms of common mental health conditions;
- use the types of information and techniques commonly found in other psychological interventions;
- deliver content through different media (such as mobile application, website, book, video or audio recording); and
- can be offered with or without guidance.
Guided self-help interventions give people some type of support in using the self-help content. Support is minimal and may include introducing the intervention, answering questions and motivating the person. It may vary in duration and intensity. Providing support has been shown to increase retention and engagement (see section 2.2.3 Engagement).
The guided self-help model described in this manual uses trained and supervised helpers to provide weekly support contacts of approximately 15 minutes as service users complete the intervention. The helper does not act as a counsellor or therapist but is trained to provide structured support that covers recapping key content, answering intervention-related questions and reviewing and encouraging use of the skills. Helpers are supervised and are trained to ensure people's safety and refer them for extra support when needed. Annexes 1A. Summary of tasks for welcome contact, 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and 1E. Summary of tasks for end contact outline the content covered in a helper contact.

1.2.1 What is self-help?
There are many ways to deliver self-help, but they all begin with providing information to a person that is interested in using the intervention. In unguided self-help this may be as simple as a health professional giving the person a book or access to a website, with a brief introduction to the content. In other settings, an informed consent procedure and assessment may be completed to determine if the person is suitable for the self-help intervention and presents with relevant symptoms. If suitable and interested, the person's journey then continues with access to the selfhelp materials. Completion of the self-help intervention ideally includes a final assessment to evaluate the intervention's outcome and, if needed, referral to further support. For guided self-help, the person receives brief but regular support contacts to help them on their journey (Figure 1.2 Example of a person's journey through individual guided self-help).

text:
1.2.2 Why use self-help and what are some limitations?
Many practitioners may have understandable concerns about whether self-help can be offered safely and effectively. Self-help is not new; it has been used for decades, both in commercial forms (such as self-help books, videos and smartphone apps) and in health services. While self-help may not be suitable for everyone, it can play a valuable role in providing effective mental health care as part of a comprehensive service approach. This section aims to provide information to address some common concerns.

The evidence
- The WHO World mental health report highlights the evidence for self-help interventions and the important role they can play in delivering evidence-based interventions to people living with mental health problems (12).
- Systematic reviews examining self-help programmes for depression and anxiety show that they are effective in reducing symptoms (13, 14). Guided self-help interventions probably have a greater effect than unguided interventions for most mental health conditions and have been shown to be as effective as in-person treatments (3, 13, 15). Additionally, self-help interventions have proven effective in various contexts, including in low- and middle-income countries (16, 17) and nationally at scale as an integral part of the health service.
- Recent WHO guidelines recommend psychological self-help interventions for depression, anxiety, bodily distress complaints, and alcohol and substance use disorders, and for carers of persons with dementia, psychosis or bipolar disorder (1).
- A guided version of SbS has been tested through two large RCTs in Lebanon and found to effectively reduce symptoms of common mental health conditions (Box 1.1 Step-by-Step in Lebanon). It has also been part of research trials for Filipino overseas workers in China (18) and Chinese young adults in Macao Special Administrative Region, China (19).
- SbS without guidance (unguided) was evaluated in Syrian refugees in Egypt, showing small positive effects in reducing psychological distress and improving overall functioning (20). However, the same version of unguided SbS tested in Germany and Sweden did not find a significant effect, suggesting the importance of considering the needs of communities when deciding on implementing interventions with or without guidance (21).
- DWM has demonstrated improvements in common mental health symptoms at immediate post-test in a pilot RCT and as part of RCTs testing a stepped-care model (22-24).

The evidence
- Other studies show the effectiveness of other self-help interventions. For example, in Indonesia an RCT of a digital guided self-help intervention reduced symptoms of depression and improved chances of remission at 10 weeks (25). Studies of the internationally used digital self-help intervention MoodGYM have similarly shown improvement in the mental health of users (26).

Box 1.1 Step-by-Step in Lebanon
In 2020, amid multiple economic, humanitarian, political and health crises in Lebanon, a culturally adapted version of SbS was tested with people living in Lebanon, including displaced Syrians, through two large RCTs. The trials showed that the intervention was effective in reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety and improving functioning and well-being, including at three-month follow-up. The trials also showed that this intervention could be delivered safely, with procedures developed to ensure support to people at imminent risk of suicide.
Step-by-Step was later scaled up as a national service in Lebanon and made available to anyone in the country. People who completed the programme said it was relevant, acceptable and beneficial.
"I encouraged one lady I know who is going through a lot in her life to enter the app. [A] few weeks later she called me and said 'I was dead and now I feel alive … if I didn't have SbS I would have definitely caused harm to myself by now.' She said the exercises helped her be socially active again and meet new friends." (Syrian outreach volunteer)
"During the Beirut explosion, when blood was running on my head, I started breathing slowly. I understand now the importance of these exercises." (Syrian woman)
"Participating in Step-by-Step was a source of strength and trust for me. I learnt how to help myself when I'm feeling sad. I learnt as well to live each day by day. The most important thing is to be myself and love myself regardless." (Lebanese woman)
Sources: Cuijpers et al. (10); Cuijpers et al. (27); Abi Ramia et al. (28).
In addition to having a strong evidence base, self-help interventions share many of the benefits of other psychological interventions delivered by non-specialists (for example, Problem Management Plus). For example, delivery by non-specialists may increase coverage and access, and free up the time of mental health specialists to provide training, supervision and interventions to people most in need. Self-help interventions can also be:

Box 1.1 Step-by-Step in Lebanon
- Practical. They give people, including those experiencing severe distress, tools and information to help self-manage mental health conditions.
- Accessible. They can be provided remotely (including for persons with mobility constraints) to large numbers of people, across large geographical areas, including hard-to-reach places (such as conflict zones). Their flexibility can reduce physical, economic, and time- or stigmarelated access barriers. They have been found to be feasible during health crises and pandemic lockdowns.
- Less resource intensive. Self-help interventions typically take less helper time to deliver than other non-specialist interventions. By delivering guided self-help remotely, helpers and supervisors can be centralized in a limited number of areas, which may help implementation or reduce costs.
- Versatile. They can be delivered locally through self-help books; or nationally, for example through a website, app or online video, with or without in-person or remote support. They can also be combined with more intensive interventions and delivered as a first step in stepped care or as a prevention intervention.
- Scalable. They can be adapted to local needs, languages and cultural contexts and reach more people than conventional in-person treatments.
Self-help interventions do have some limitations:
- Commercially available self-help interventions may not be evidence based. It is important to check the background and evidence behind any self-help intervention before providing it to populations in need (see section 2.1.1 Intervention selection).
- They may not be right for all people (see section 1.2.3 Who is self-help for?) and should be part of a range of services, rather than a stand-alone approach.
- They usually have higher drop-out rates than face-to-face interventions (see section 2.2.3 Engagement).
The above limitations all highlight the importance of incorporating self-help interventions as part of a comprehensive system.

1.2.3 Who is self-help for?
Self-help interventions are often developed and tested to benefit people with specific mental health conditions (such as depression) or symptoms that may cross a range of mental health conditions ("transdiagnostic" interventions). Some self-help interventions do not focus on a specific mental health condition but rather aim to increase psychological well-being.
Self-help interventions can be used by different populations, including people:
- of different beliefs, religions and cultural backgrounds;
- with varying levels of education (although ability to read, use a digital device or access the internet may be required, depending on format); and
- from different age groups (preferably interventions for specific age groups are co-designed and tested with people from these age groups; however, in some cases interventions have been adapted for other age groups; see section 2.2 Adapt for context and culture).
Most self-help interventions are not designed for people with severe cognitive impairments, such as those related to a mental, neurological or substance use disorder. Most are not designed for people in high-risk situations, such as imminent risk of suicide, or harm through intimate partner violence or abuse. People facing these risks may benefit from self-help but only if the risk situation is adequately addressed. Similarly, people with additional needs, such as comorbid health conditions, protection concerns or housing problems, may benefit from self-help but should also be referred for extra support, for example from other health, social service or protection agencies.
This manual focuses on interventions that are developed to treat mental health conditions. When selecting an intervention it is important to choose one that targets the population you want to help (see section 2.1.1 Intervention selection).

1.2.4. Where can self-help be used?
Self-help interventions can be offered at local, regional or national levels, and can be provided using in-person or remote support, including call centres or helplines. They suit various settings but are particularly useful for places where geographical, financial or resource constraints limit access to mental health services. Intervention use may have specific requirements, such as the ability to read or access the internet. When planning to implement self-help, it is important to consider any potential barriers to access (including literacy, digital literacy, access to digital devices and internet connectivity).
It is also important to consider how self-help interventions can be embedded in local health care and protection systems. As with all psychological interventions, appropriate referral and support options for both mental health concerns (for example, access to a clinician trained under the Mental Health Gap Action Programme (MhGAP) or referral to a local specialized service) and protection concerns (for example, in the case of gender-based violence or violence against children) should be available. If you are implementing self-help interventions, it is critical that funding is available not only for the self-help interventions, but also to ensure that access to these and other services is possible. Self-help interventions can complement other forms of care, such as more intensive psychological interventions or medicines, by providing additional tools and strategies for managing symptoms.
Interventions such as SbS and DWM generally use community providers specifically recruited to serve as helpers, for example undergraduates, community members, lay volunteers and peers. Yet other providers, including primary health care providers or trained clinicians, can also support people with self-help interventions. They may not have the time to deliver the 15 minutes of weekly support outlined in the DWM and SbS model, but they could be trained to provide a self-help book and check in on the person's use of its strategies as part of routine follow-up appointments. The guidance in this manual can be adapted for such settings.
Note. For more detailed information on how to set up psychological interventions, including self-help interventions, see the WHO Psychological interventions implementation manual (29).

1.2.5 When to use guided or unguided self-help
Guided self-help is likely to be more effective than unguided self-help (3, 15). Yet implementing guided self-help may not always be feasible because of the programme's aims or resource constraints. Unguided self-help can still benefit people, especially when delivered across a large population. The impact of an intervention can be considered as a combination of the effectiveness in reducing symptoms and the number of people reached. A guided self-help intervention may be more effective for individuals but will probably reach fewer people. The opposite is true for unguided self-help, although a 2021 systematic review of self-help interventions for depression suggested that guided and unguided self-help interventions may be similarly effective for people with mild symptoms (30). It is always important to consider the intervention that is planned, and how it matches the needs of populations.
Delivering guided self-help requires more financial and human resources than unguided self-help, specifically to set up and run the team of helpers. But regular contact with a helper has many benefits. As well as supporting people to adhere to and complete the intervention and so increase its effectiveness, it gives people regular opportunities for human contact, assessment and referral (see section 2.1.3 Support models for guided self-help for more information on support models and what is needed to provide guidance).
Choosing guided or unguided self-help is not necessarily an either/or decision. There are many options. For example, a programme or service may:
- start by providing unguided self-help and add a guided component when resources become available;
- offer guided self-help where needs are high and offer unguided self-help elsewhere; or
- offer unguided self-help to people with less severe symptoms and offer guided self-help to people with more severe symptoms.

2. For organizations: how to set up individually delivered self-help
This chapter is primarily written for people responsible for developing or implementing individually delivered self-help interventions. If you want information on being a helper, supervisor or trainer you may want to skip to Chapter 3. Introduction to providing support in guided self-help.
Note. In the sections that follow, we set out the key activities to conduct when implementing individually delivered self-help, in line with WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual (29). The implementation manual provides the information needed for planning and implementing psychological interventions delivered by non-specialists and should be read alongside this document.
While this manual focuses mainly on individually delivered guided self-help and providing remote support, information covered in this chapter is also relevant for providing individually delivered unguided self-help or in-person support.
Planning for self-help involves making some key decisions before working out an implementation plan. Information needed to make some of these decisions was discussed in Chapter 1, and other key points will be covered here. A checklist for planning and implementing psychological interventions can be found in Annex 1 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual.

2.1 Plan for individually delivered self-help
WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual identifies seven key activities for planning psychological interventions (Figure 2.1 Seven key questions to address in an implementation plan).
Figure 2.1 Seven key questions to address in an implementation plan

<!-- image -->
Source: WHO (29).
In this section we offer additional information on four of the activities, as these have specific considerations for self-help interventions. It is important to include multiple stakeholders, including community representatives (such as community leaders and people with mental health conditions) in the planning and implementation team.
It is recommended that an implementation plan be developed in the planning phase to ensure that all key questions are addressed (see Annex 1 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual for a checklist of key activities in planning for the implementation of a psychological intervention).

2.1.1 Intervention selection
The choice of intervention is informed by a first step of identifying local needs, capacities and priorities. The intervention content should target the mental health conditions identified as local priorities, but always as part of a comprehensive system.
It is important to review the evidence for the intervention to ensure its likely effectiveness. Gathering service user feedback is also critical to ensure that the intervention aligns with people's needs and preferences, for example with regard to literacy, access to digital devices, preferred medium of communication, or use of individual or group interventions. This feedback will guide the choice of intervention and whether an individual guided or unguided intervention is selected, or another form of self-help such as Self-Help Plus (SH+) (31).
The following information relates to individually delivered self-help interventions.
Some digital self-help interventions (both online and through mobile apps) may not have been tested for effectiveness, so it is important to check what evidence supports them. Interventions may be proven effective only for a specific population group, yet this evidence can often be generalized across genders and some age groups (32). Most evidence-based self-help interventions have been developed and tested for people aged over 18 years, but there is a growing number of interventions for younger people. While using an intervention designed for and tested with young people is preferred, in some cases interventions have been adapted for and implemented in other age groups. See WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual for more information on adapting interventions (29).
WHO has developed two individually delivered self-help interventions, SbS and DWM, that have been tested, evaluated and proven to have a positive effect on mental health. Table 2.1 gives an overview of their characteristics. Chapters 5 and 6 give more information on SbS and DWM. The interventions use a similar format (illustrated self-help), but have different content that may require differing levels of adaptation. A first step in deciding whether to use DWM or SbS is reading through the content in full.

2.1.1 Intervention selection
Table 2.1 Overview of SbS and DWM

| | SbS (see Chapter 5) | DWM (see Chapter 6) |
| - | - | - |
| Target population | Adults with moderate to severe depressive symptoms. | Adults experiencing psychological distress of various levels of severity. |
| Main therapeutic components | Behavioural activation, stress management and other techniques. | Acceptance and commitment therapy. DWM is the book component of Self-Help Plus (SH+) (31) and includes all of the same self-help techniques and content. It has subsequently been used and tested as a stand-alone individually delivered intervention. |
| Format | Digital, but could be delivered in different formats, such as a book or video. | Digital and book, but could be delivered in different formats, such as a video. |
| Length | Five modules. | Five modules. |
| Guidance | One welcome contact and five weekly support contacts of 15 minutes per week. | Tested with both five weekly support contacts and three support contacts over five weeks of 15 minutes. |
| Adaptation | SbS follows individual storylines developed for different genders and age groups, including a young person story. This helps it feel more personalized but increases the amount of content to adapt. | DWM follows a group of narrators explaining key concepts. Images are already adapted for multiple cultures and text is short, so the amount of adaptation required may be more limited. |

2.1.1 Intervention selection
| | SbS (see Chapter 5) | DWM (see Chapter 6) |
| - | - | - |
| Current strength of evidence | Two RCTs in Lebanon showed moderate effects on mental health outcomes that were maintained at three-month follow- up (10, 27). An RCT with an adapted version of SbS with Chinese students showed it effectively reduced depressive symptoms in the short term and improved psychological well-being in the longer term (19). One trial with an unguided version of SbS in Syrian refugees in Egypt showed small effects that remained at three-month follow-up (20), while another trial with the same population in Germany and Sweden did not find an effect (21). | One published pilot trial showing small to moderate pre-post effects on symptoms (22). Two published trials showing moderate pre-post effects on symptoms, as part of a stepped care trial (11, 23). One published pre-post (not RCT) paper on unguided DWM showed significant effects in reducing symptoms of depression, anxiety and distress and improved well-being in over 1400 students in Italy (33). |

2.1.2 Delivery options
Several planning activities in WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual are about deciding how to deliver a psychological intervention. For self-help, this includes deciding whether to offer the intervention with or without guidance (or both depending on symptom severity); and deciding what format and media to use (for both content and guidance).
Self-help can be delivered using different models with different levels of guidance. For example, it may be:
- made available to all adults in a community affected by adversity, with no guidance (for example, a self-help book made available in public spaces);
- provided by primary health care workers and others as part of routine care for people with mental health conditions (including significant psychological distress), with brief check-ins during regular follow-up appointments;
- open to all adults in a community affected by adversity, with guidance offered to those who score above the cut-off value on a measure of depression or psychological distress; 4
- combined with other forms of psychological treatment, for example as part of stepped care, whereby people are offered progressively intensive treatments based on clinical need.
The content in both guided and unguided self-help can be delivered through different media, including a physical book, a mobile application or website, a PDF document, or a series of videos or audio recordings (such as podcasts). Feedback from service users on what they can use or would prefer is very important here (see section 2.2.1 Adapting the intervention on adapting the intervention).
If you choose to deliver a digital intervention or deliver self-help remotely, you will need to ensure that:
- potential service users have access to the internet, a suitable device (smartphone, tablet or computer), and, depending on the registration process, an email address or phone number; and
- the intervention is accessible for people with older mobile devices and slower or unstable internet connections. Making the application usable offline and giving choices on what to download can help make the intervention more inclusive.

2.1.2 Delivery options
For digital interventions, you will also need to ensure that sufficient resources and skills are available to implement, host and maintain a digital delivery platform that secures any personal information and is compliant with any local regulations. Digital resources may be delivered on their own platform or potentially using existing and widely used platforms (such as YouTube or WhatsApp). Key requirements for many digital interventions include:
- a technical strategy based on user needs and preferences to inform the technical design and architecture;
4 Contact psych\_interventions@who.int for more information.
- a secure mobile application or website (such as an e-learning platform);
- technical capacity to host, maintain and update a digital platform;
- a system to register and support service users with technical issues (such as resetting passwords); and
- policies and practices to ensure compliance with local rules and regulations on data protection, security, use of digital health devices and any other relevant areas.
If the digital self-help intervention includes guidance, additional requirements may include:
- telephones or access to a secure digital video or messaging platform to contact service users; and
- a case record system to record information about the support contacts (such as duration and what was discussed).
There are numerous ways in which SbS, DWM and other evidence-based, individually delivered, psychological self-help interventions can be implemented as part of a comprehensive system of care. For example, you may choose to:
- implement one or the other intervention based on priority problems in your area;
- implement both interventions and direct people to each one depending on their symptoms; or
- provide self-help as a first step in stepped care.
This decision will in large part depend on the needs of the population and the resources available.

2.1.3 Support models for guided self-help
In guided self-help, support and motivation is provided by a person trained to give this guidance. This may be as part of routine appointments, but often it is provided by trained and supervised helpers recruited for this purpose. They provide encouragement, answer questions about the intervention and its content, and make referrals when required.
The following information relates primarily to situations where non-specialist helpers are recruited for this role.
Support can be delivered remotely or in person, either in real time (live support) or with a time delay using pre-recorded voice or written messages (delayed support).
Live support (also called "synchronous" support) happens through a live conversation, typically during a pre-booked appointment slot. Contact can be by telephone, video, instant messaging or in person. Live support is useful because:
- the service user can ask follow-up questions or get immediate clarifications, which can help them progress through the intervention;
- the regular appointment may increase motivation to continue with the intervention; and
- the communication may feel more natural and supportive.
Potential challenges include helpers needing practice to keep support contacts brief (a problem addressed in training and supervision). Remote live support is also only possible with stable internet or phone connections.
Delayed support (also called "asynchronous" support) occurs when the conversation between the helper and the service user is not completed in real time (that is, they leave messages for a response later). The helper will still allocate time to sending their support messages, but this will not be a live conversation. The advantages of this approach are that:
- it is convenient, as service users can choose when and where to engage with the support;
- it may give people time to think about their message and response;
- it is time efficient and less burdensome for helpers as they can work with (adapted) templates; and
- it creates a record (either written or audio, if voice messages are used).

2.1.3 Support models for guided self-help
The main drawback of delayed support is that it may feel less natural or engaging than a live call. Yet communication preferences vary across cultures, so for some service users (such as young people) it may be preferred. Delayed support also requires clear communication to ensure service users do not confuse the contact with a live chat and expect to get a direct response. An automatic response reminding people that helpers will reply within a given time frame will help manage communication expectations. When using delayed support, people should be aware of what to do in a crisis situation (for example, imminent risk of suicide or other protection concerns) and there should be a system in place for responding urgently, and with live support (such as a telephone call), to any messages that indicate such risks.
In some of the research for guided versions of both SbS and DWM, service users were offered the choice of live support (talking to the same helper on the telephone for 15 minutes each week) or delayed support (receiving a text or voice message). Most people chose telephone-based support - but having the choice was seen as important. While the evidence clearly shows that guided interventions are effective, there is little research on the different effects of different support types, such as live or delayed support, or telephone or message.
To increase the chance that implementation results reflect trial results, you should use a similar support model as used in the research. For SbS and DWM, this would mean using the support models described in Chapters 3-6 of this manual. Yet this can be adapted to context. Example adaptations include reducing or increasing the number of contacts, using a different technology to provide support (for example, live voice notes rather than telephone calls) or offering support on demand.
Ideally, any adaptations to the support model should be piloted before full implementation to determine whether the intervention remains engaging and effective.

2.1.3 Support models for guided self-help
Before deciding what support model to use, consider the technology available in your region, preferred methods of communication within your target population, human resources available and amount of people you want to reach, as well as user feedback on preferences. See Annex 1. Summary of tasks for different contacts, and example scripts and texts for a summary of tasks for the different support contacts and example templates for live and delayed support that you can adapt for use in your context.

2.1.4 Human resource needs
Within all delivery and support models you will need to consider your human resource needs. The simplest form of guided self-help (not explicitly covered in this manual) is for a service provider to give people access to the self-help material and then check in during routine appointments (covering some of the topics listed in section 4.2 Regular support contacts).
To implement SbS or DWM, you will need a team of people to carry out various tasks (Table 2.2). This team could comprise people already employed by the organization or those specifically hired to deliver individually delivered self-help.
Table 2.2 Example tasks needed to implement a programme of guided self-help interventions using the WHO model described in this manual

| Task | Example roles and responsibilities |
| - | - |
| Coordination | · Manage the programme of self-help · Assess the quality of the programme's implementation · Oversee the programme's administrative and operational elements (including monitoring and evaluation) · Ensure helpers are recruited and trained · Allocate helpers to service users at sign-up |
| Providing support | · Give service users brief support and encouragement as they progress through the intervention · Maintain privacy · Respond to any safety or protection concerns, such as imminent risk of suicide · (See section 3.1 for more information on what it means to be a helper) |
| Supervision | · Provide training and support to helpers · Ensure that support is delivered competently and safely · Follow up on any safety or protection concerns |
| IT support (for digital intervention) | · Ensure hosting and maintenance of the intervention · Provide helpers and service users with technical support |
When delivering interventions remotely, it is important to develop clear rules and practices (also called standard operating procedures) for how helpers contact service users and make case notes. For example, helpers should only contact service users using work devices, during working hours and in ways that ensure the safety and privacy both of themselves and of the people they are helping (that is, not making calls from home).

2.1.4 Human resource needs
Even when delivering self-help interventions remotely, it can be useful to have the team of helpers working in a centralized location to create a supportive atmosphere.
For information on how to prepare the team through recruitment, training and supervision, see section 2.3 Prepare the workforce.

2.1.5 Monitoring and evaluation
As with implementing all psychological interventions, it is essential to make a monitoring and evaluation plan to effectively measure the impact of implementing self-help interventions.
For information on making a plan and important indicators for psychological interventions, see WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual (29).

2.2 Adapt for context and culture
Before implementing your chosen self-help intervention, you should consider how well it fits the local context and culture of your target population, and adapt it where necessary to maximize engagement and effectiveness. Chapter 3 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual sets out the goals of and strategies for adaptation of diverse psychological interventions (29).

2.2.1 Adapting the intervention
The adaptation of self-help interventions may involve changes to both their content and format. For example, if the intervention is being delivered for a specific population or situation, such as health care workers during a pandemic, the content (such as illustrations) may need adapting to reflect those experiences (34). If the intervention follows a story, as in the case of SbS, then characters and parts of the story may be changed to make them more culturally appropriate or to address contextspecific stressors and experiences (Box 2.1). For example, depending on the context, a doctor character that provides psychoeducational content can be replaced with another trusted, culturally appropriate character, for example a health care professional, a community helper, a community elder or a peer. Language translation and updates to audio or visual content will be necessary to ensure cultural appropriateness.
When adapting self-help interventions that use substantial illustrations, audio scripts or videos, adopting an iterative approach may help reduce errors that would be costly to fix later on. Digital interventions are particularly difficult and expensive to change in later stages. Rather than redrawing all illustrations or re-recording an entire audio intervention, try adapting one section at a time, testing each one with the local community before moving on to the next section. This will help get the language, tone and visual presentation of the intervention right. It is also important to make selfhelp materials fun and easy to use, as there is limited human contact to ensure adherence. Looking at television adverts or radio shows can give an idea of the warmth or tone needed for self-help materials.
Piloting the adapted intervention with a small number of service users first is advised. This will give information about how well the adaptations work and if there is a need to make more adaptations.

Box 2.1 Examples of SbS adapted for local context
SbS uses narrative stories with illustrations. It has been adapted for various target populations using a cultural adaptation process involving substantial engagement with local community members and other stakeholders.
Lebanese, Syrian refugees and other populations in Lebanon. a SbS, in collaboration with the National Mental Health Programme at Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health, was adapted following interviews with the target population to reflect gender, language and cultural nuances among different populations. Two male and female versions were developed, which share the same content but feature different illustrated characters representing Lebanon's main cultural groups. Exercise examples were revised to reflect local experiences. To increase acceptability, service users choose their preferred method, day and time of contact with a helper.
Filipino migrant workers. b Filipino overseas workers in Macao Special Administrative Region, China, reported several issues with the generic version of SbS. Key adaptations to address these included changing the narrative to match Filipino experiences and values; changing some activities so they were more familiar to overseas Filipino workers; changing the main character from a doctor to a wise elder; and simplifying and translating the text, including by using a mix of English and Filipino, where appropriate.
Chinese young adults. c Based on feedback from focus group discussions, changes were made
to the language, narratives and characters used, as well as some of the concepts and exercises. This included adding scenarios related to university life, changing the main character from a doctor to a peer, changing expressions to fit young adults' experiences and translating the intervention into both traditional and simplified Chinese.
Thailand: integration into the Tor-Tuem-Jai Programme. d Thailand has integrated two WHO tools - Step-by-Step (SbS) and Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM) - into a unified digital platform called Tor-Tuem-Jai. The content was carefully adapted through a four-stage process to ensure cultural relevance, including redesigning characters and illustrations, consulting experts and refining materials based on community feedback.

2.2.2 Adapting protocols and guidance materials
Besides adapting the intervention content and format, it is important to adapt all the protocols and guidance given to helpers and supervisors to the local context.
The information provided in Chapter 3. Introduction to providing support in guided self-help (on how to provide support in individually delivered guided self-help) is based on the approach used to run SbS and DWM. Many sections state that further information will be provided by the implementing organization. As the programme manager or implementing organization, it is important for you to read through Chapter 3 and adapt the approach to your own organization and setting before sharing the information with helpers.
It is especially important to adapt (or develop) protocols or guidance for helpers on how to:
- manage safety and protection concerns;
- refer people in need of other support or services;
- deal with unsuccessful contacts;
- deal with a friend or family member who calls to ask about the intervention; and
- remind service users to complete any final questionnaires and inform them about any further follow-ups or assessments.
It is also important to ensure you have protocols or guidance for coordinators, for example on how to monitor and evaluate the service (including which measures to use and when).
If you are using any of the tools and templates provided in the annexes to this manual (for example, the list of supporting organizations for referral, contact templates and supervision materials), these will also need adapting to your context before being shared with the self-help intervention team.

2.2.3 Engagement
The intervention will also need to be adapted to ensure it is as engaging as possible to the population you want to reach. Self-help interventions often have lower adherence and engagement rates than interventions delivered fully by a person. Dropping out - that is, not finishing the intervention - is common in mental health interventions, but may be higher in self-help interventions (40). For example, a meta-analysis of digital interventions for depression reported that on average 25% of participants completed the intervention when delivered in routine clinical settings (41).
There is limited evidence on what exactly increases adherence (42). In general, it seems that adding guidance to the self-help intervention increases adherence (43). Also, ensuring that the intervention is adapted to the needs and context of the population will increase the chances that people are more engaged.
In the design of digital self-help interventions, adding features such as nudges, reminders and mood tracking may increase adherence. For example, adding a mood monitor to smartphone interventions has been shown to lower drop-out (44).

2.3 Prepare the workforce
Chapter 4 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual provides information on preparing the workforce, including tips and tools for recruiting, training and supervising helpers (29). In addition, WHO's Ensuring Quality in Psychological Support (EQUIP) initiative gives information on how competency-based training and assessment can be integrated (45).
The sections that follow focus on extra information that is particularly relevant to guided self-help and are based on the SbS and DWM model tested in research trials. In this manual, a "helper" refers to a non-specialist.

2.3.1 Recruitment
Supervisors and trainers are ideally mental health professionals who are competent and experienced in delivering psychological interventions or guided self-help. In some contexts this will not be feasible, and people who do not have a mental health background but are trained and experienced in providing guided self-help interventions can be trainers or supervisors under the supervision of a mental health professional.
When planning recruitment, think about how many helpers, supervisors and trainers you will need, what their working hours will be and what a manageable caseload for helpers might be. Helpers typically need at least 30 minutes per service user per contact, which includes preparation time, the 15-minute contact and writing up case notes. Time should also be available for attending supervision sessions. Manageable caseloads vary by context, so you will need to consider what is appropriate in your setting.

2.3.2 Training
Training to support guided self-help can be quicker than for some other psychological interventions. This is because in guided self-help, helpers do not have to explain concepts in depth or engage with people for extended periods of time. Training is however still essential. WHO recommends taking a competency-based training approach. For more information on competency-based training see WHO's Ensuring Quality in Psychological Support (EQUIP) initiative (45) and section 4.2 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual (29).
Training generally happens in three stages:
- Preparation: becoming familiar with the intervention's content and materials.
- Workshop: attending an interactive training workshop, which includes hands-on practice of helper skills. The duration of the workshop will depend on the intervention. Training for SbS and DWM each take four to five days.
- Practice and ongoing supervision: doing practice cases and delivering the intervention to real service users, while receiving ongoing supervision and support.
Training manuals for SbS and DWM will be published by WHO. 5

2.3.3 Supportive supervision
Supervisors are ultimately responsible for ensuring that the intervention - including the support given by helpers - is delivered competently and safely. Supportive supervision ensures that helpers provide quality interventions and continue developing and refining their helping skills.
Section 4.3 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual describes the components of supportive supervision and sets out different options for how, where and how often to provide it (29).
The level of supervision required by helpers will vary according to their level of expertise and experience. For example, lay volunteers who are new to providing help for mental health problems may need a lot of supervision, while a doctor in primary care who is used to talking to people with mental health problems may need limited supervision when providing self-help.
In the research trials of SbS and DWM, supervisors met their helpers (non-specialists) regularly, typically in a group, for around 60-90 minutes once a week or fortnightly. Those experiences suggested that supervision was especially valuable to support helpers in keeping their contacts brief and learning how to manage people who were expecting a therapy session or who wanted or needed more support than could be provided.
5 Contact psych\_interventions@who.int for more information.

2.4 Helping people to access self-help
Before, during and after participating in self-help, it is important for people to receive the support they need. Key questions to consider include:
- How and where will the intervention be advertised or promoted?
- Where will referrals come from, and how does this fit into existing services?
- How will people access the self-help intervention? For example, will they need a referral from an existing service? Or will they fill out an online questionnaire and be automatically referred based on their results?
- How and where will people with extra support needs be referred to or informed about other services and supports?
As with all psychological interventions, appropriate referral and support options for both mental health concerns (for example, access to a trained mhGAP clinician or referral to a local specialized service) and protection concerns (for example, gender-based violence and violence against children) should be available. When implementing self-help interventions, it is important to map out available services (such as health, rehabilitation, education, protection and social services) and build or strengthen multisectoral links for referral. Referral options for people at imminent risk of suicide and for people with severe mental, neurological or substance use conditions must be in place. When referral options are limited, they can be created by training and supervising general health care providers to assess and manage mental, neurological and substance use conditions in the local health system, for example through mhGAP.
Chapter 5 of WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual describes how to identify, treat and follow up potential users of a psychological intervention - including how to refer people to other services if the intervention is not suitable - to ensure that people get the support they need (29). When implementing guided self-help there are some other points to consider, as described below.

text:
2.4.1 Identifying, assessing and engaging people for self-help
For some self-help interventions, including SbS, it is important to identify potential beneficiaries by some form of case detection through initial assessment or screening. This ensures:
- a match between what the person needs and what the intervention can provide;
- that the intervention is offered to those most likely to benefit from it; and
- that people who may need extra support - for example, because they are at imminent risk of suicide, self-harm or harm from others - are identified and referred appropriately.
Screening and assessment will vary by context but aims to identify people who may be in need of, and benefit from, the intervention. For example, in self-help this may be done as part of routine clinical care, by screening people in the community who are identified as being at risk of the particular problem (such as depression), or online, by people accessing the screening tool after seeing a message or post advertising the intervention. Screening and assessment may be done in person or online. They may be done together or as part of a multistep process in which initial case detection is followed by further assessment where indicated (Box 2.2 Example process for online screening and assessment based on SbS and DWM). For more information on case detection methods see WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual (29).

text:
Step 1. Screen for suitability based on a validated measure
Screening can be done using a locally validated measure of psychological distress or symptoms of common mental health conditions, such as depression and anxiety. a If the intervention is being delivered through a digital platform, screening may be done as part of the sign-up process.
You should choose your own screening criteria and outcome based on your local context and intended use of the intervention. You might decide to:
- only provide the intervention to people who score above the cut-off value; or
- provide the intervention as guided to people who score above a certain cut-off value but still offer the intervention, in an unguided format, to everyone else.
Screening should include questions to assess whether the person has other support needs or whether there is any reason to exclude them from the intervention. This includes questions to assess for imminent risk of suicide, self-harm or any other protection concerns or needs that may require a higher level of care (such as substance dependence or psychosis). These screening questionnaires can be delivered in many ways, for example by a trained and supervised non-specialist as with other WHO psychological interventions, or online, potentially with a follow-up call to discuss the results of the screening. Decisions on how to respond to these should be based on local procedures and policies. For example, people indicating a possible need for additional services should receive a referral for these. Similarly, in online screening, people who indicate imminent risk of suicide or other protection concerns may receive a follow-up contact from a programme manager. Once the imminent risk has been managed, they can still be invited to join the intervention.

Step 3. End of programme assessment
At the end of the self-help programme, the assessment measures should be repeated. Depending on local resources, their results can be used to determine whether the person needs further support and for monitoring and evaluation purposes. The outcomes across a range of people might also suggest the need for further adaptation of the intervention.
- a Examples of locally validated measures include the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) and the Kessler 6 (K-6).
In guided self-help, after screening and assessment, anyone suitable for the guided selfhelp intervention must be allocated to a helper for support, through an agreed method of communication (which may be based on personal preference).
Providing clear information about the intervention is an important part of the screening and assessment process. Individuals need to understand what the programme involves and what to expect. This information can be delivered through the intervention itself (for example, in a mobile app or website) or by the person introducing it (for example, a helper or health professional). Because self-help interventions are easy to access, people may sign up without a full understanding of the commitment required. Experience with SbS and DWM suggests that a call or contact with everyone who registers to use the programme, even if completed without guidance, may increase engagement and reduce drop-out by allowing people to ask questions and decide if the programme is right for them. Similar to other psychological interventions, an informed consent procedure should take place after providing information about the intervention.
For more information on recruitment and identification of people for self-help see WHO's Psychological interventions implementation manual (29).

2.4.2 Addressing safety and protection concerns
The system for responding to safety and protection concerns (such as imminent risk of suicide or harm from others) and for connecting people to external services and support will depend on local policies and practices, as well as how the intervention is being provided (online, remote or in person). If an intervention is being delivered remotely, extra care may be needed to ensure adequate response to safety and protection concerns. To support helpers manage risk remotely, together with a mental health specialist, consider developing policies, protocols or training on:
- how to create a safety plan in the first remote support contact, where required;
- how to establish where the service user is during a support contact and whether they are safe; and
- how to respond to emergency situations such as imminent risk of suicide (for example, having contact information for referral services, such as emergency health services or a health clinic with staff trained in mhGAP).
See Annexes 2A. Service user experiences distress during a contact and 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact for example protocols (that can be adapted to your context) for assessing and responding to cases of imminent risk of suicide or self-harm, and cases of sexual assault or intimate partner violence.

2.4.3 Managing caseloads and follow-up
One challenge with self-help interventions is that drop-out can be very high, especially at the start of online interventions. This is because the threshold and effort to sign up are very low.
Consider what will happen if someone stops engaging in the intervention, and decide:
- how many missed appointments or contact attempts will be allowed before helpers can stop contacting the person;
- what will be done with people who want to pause the intervention for some time; and
- how much time people can take to complete the intervention and receive support from a helper.
These questions are important to avoid helpers developing full caseloads of people who are not engaging with the intervention. It may be helpful to have someone in the service whose role it is to contact people before they are assigned to a helper and added to the caseload. Establishing early contact and providing an opportunity for people to ask questions about the intervention may help reduce the number of early drop-outs, as it improves informed consent and helps manage expectations.
Also consider what will happen when people finish the intervention, particularly if they are still experiencing high levels of distress (see section 4.3 End contact). Have helpers or the intervention platform repeat the screening measure at discharge to monitor change and identify people who need further support. A system is needed to track participants, record case notes and manage appointments.

text:
3. Introduction to providing support in guided self-help
This chapter is primarily written for helpers who support people through a guided self-help intervention. Programme managers may also find it useful to get a thorough understanding of how helper guidance should work in practice.
In the sections that follow, we outline the general support model used in RCTs for SbS and DWM (10, 23). It assumes that, as in the trials, helpers will be non-specialists with limited or no previous experience of working in mental health care. Much of the information here may also be helpful to health care providers delivering guided self-help as part of routine appointments.
As with other parts of this manual, the advice given below can and should be adapted to specific organizational needs. For example, it assumes you are providing remote support, but can easily be adapted for in-person support. Similarly, it recommends weekly contacts with the helper, but implementing organizations may have good reason to change the frequency of contacts. For example, there is early evidence that DWM is effective with only three contacts (at the start, after two weeks and at the end) (22). Even if you are not planning to use SbS or DWM, you can use the advice in this manual to help plan and implement other evidence-based guided self-help.
Chapters 5 and 6 of this manual offer specific tips and tools on how to support people through SbS and DWM. A training manual for SbS and DWM helpers will be published by WHO and will give further information on how helpers should provide support for these interventions. 6
Note for programme managers. Many sections in this chapter suggest that further information will be provided by the implementing organization. Please read through this chapter and adapt the approach to your setting before sharing any information with helpers.

metadata.heading_path: 3.1 What does it mean to be a helper?
