text:
3.1 What does it mean to be a helper?
Helpers are trained to support people through a psychological intervention (including guided selfhelp). Helpers are not like professional therapists who give people counselling or advice. Instead, they work alongside a self-help intervention. The intervention provides the therapeutic content; helpers are there to offer brief, regular support to keep people on track, help them with any problems they encounter, and steer them through the intervention. They communicate with service users through real-time conversations or pre-recorded voice or written messages (see section 2.1.3 Support models for guided self-help).
6 Contact psych\_interventions@who.int for more information.
Your implementing organization will tell you which type of support to provide, when and for how long. In Annex 1. Summary of tasks for different contacts, and example scripts and texts you will find a series of templates to help you provide support (although you should always personalize these to the person you are helping).

Box 3.1 Addressing safety concerns
Helpers are not solely responsible for managing safety concerns, such as imminent risk of suicide.
Your role in these situations is to identify the safety concern, follow the protocol and inform your supervisor. Your supervisor will have sufficient skills and training to manage the situation. They are ultimately responsible for ensuring people's safety as they complete the guided self-help.
See section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns? for more information.

3.1.2 Ethics and principles
Helpers must have a good understanding of the local culture. Cultures can vary enormously within countries, regions and communities, and it is important to be aware of potential differences. This is something you can talk to your supervisor about (46).
Some helpers (for example, health professionals) may belong to a regulated health profession. If this is the case, you need to follow the ethical standards and guidelines of that profession. All helpers need to treat all service users with respect, regardless of their characteristics, including age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, culture, religion, political beliefs, race, ethnicity, physical or mental abilities, or economic or social background. Discrimination in any form is not acceptable. Table 3.1 Some dos and don'ts of helping people through guided self-help lists some dos and don'ts of helping people through guided self-help.

3.1.3 Training and supervision
Learning to be a helper happens in three stages. It starts as soon as you sign up to be a helper and continues well after any classroom training, for as long as you continue to support people through guided self-help.

Stage I: Before classroom training
In this stage, you will:
- familiarize yourself with the intervention (for example, by reading through the self-help content and understanding the rationale for the intervention);
- complete the intervention yourself, working through every module - ideally, a knowledgeable helper can help you to experience what it is like to receive the support; and
- practise the exercises in the intervention.

Stage III: After classroom training
Even after any classroom training ends, you will continue to develop your helping skills under supportive supervision and strengthen your competency to deliver support.
- You will do practice cases, in which you will provide support to two people with mild symptoms under close supervision. If this is not possible, for example because the intervention is delivered remotely, mock cases (in which people play a role of someone in distress) can be used as an alternative.
- You will continue to use role play to help your learning.
- You will repeat the intervention yourself, and practise the exercises at home, as many times as you need to know it well.
- You will attend regular supervision and any further training that is required. Supervision is typically in a group, for around 60-90 minutes once a week or fortnightly.
Supervision is a critical part of any psychological intervention. Throughout your role as a helper, your supervisor will be there to help you build your skills and offer support and guidance, especially for difficult cases. You will not be alone.
Supervision forms can be used to prepare for supervision and think about what issues you want to raise with your supervisor (see Annex 4. Supervision templates for example supervision forms). Remember that there is no such thing as a silly question and that if you have thought it, other helpers are likely to have thought it too.
In emergency cases - such as imminent risk of suicide, self-harm or harm to or from others - you can approach your supervisor outside supervision sessions for some one-to-one support.

metadata.topic: 3.2 What helping skills do I need to be a helper?
metadata.heading_path: 3.2 What helping skills do I need to be a helper?
metadata.module: 3.2 What helping skills do I need to be a helper?
metadata.section: 3.2 What helping skills do I need to be a helper?

text:
3.2 What helping skills do I need to be a helper?
Helpers use basic helping skills (also known as foundational helping skills) to support people through guided self-help. These skills build a sense of trust, confidence and security. They help service users feel listened to, accepted and valued.
In this section we outline the basic helping skills you will need as a helper. Note that these are different from the skills that service users learn when they complete the self-help interventions, which are described in Chapters 5. Information for helpers delivering Step-by-Step and 6. Information for helpers delivering Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM) of this document.
Remember the limitations of your role: it is the self-help intervention, not you, that teaches people the skills they need to manage their mental health conditions. You are not there to be a therapist or to give people advice.

3.2.1 Communicate verbally and non-verbally
The way you communicate with someone in distress is very important; see Table 3.2 Some dos and don'ts of communicating with service users of guided self-help for some dos and don'ts of communicating with service users of guided self-help. To communicate well, you should be aware of both your words and your tone of voice; your body language, including facial expressions, eye contact and gestures; and the way you sit or stand in relation to other people.
Communicating well can be more challenging if you deliver support by telephone or written messages. But it is still possible. You should always give people your full attention and consider the tone, volume and speed of your speech and how this may be interpreted. It can help to imagine the person sitting in front of you and use your body language (such as nodding or hand gestures) as you would if they were there. This can help you keep focused and improve your verbal communication.
Remember that each culture has its own ways of behaving that are appropriate and respectful. Always speak and behave in ways that consider important characteristics, including age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, culture, religion, political beliefs, race, ethnicity, physical or mental abilities, or economic or social background.

3.2.2 Maintain confidentiality
People completing guided self-help need to know that the information they give you will remain confidential or private and will not be shared with anyone outside your team. They also need to be aware of limits to confidentiality. For example, you can share information about a person without their consent if there is a serious risk of harm to themselves or others. This includes imminent risk of suicide or self-harm, threat to life, risk of sexual violence or intimate partner violence, and child protection concerns (see section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns?).
Service users also need to be informed that you attend supervision, and that information about them might be shared with your supervisor and members of your team to ensure that they receive the best service. They may need to be reminded that everyone in your team is bound by the same confidentiality rules. Only share information with your team when you have to.
As part of maintaining confidentiality, you should keep all information about service users (such as assessment results and personal details) in a safe place. Make sure you follow your organization's rules about data security (including access, passwords, copying and forwarding information, and using company email accounts).
If delivering help remotely, you may need additional protections to ensure confidentiality (see section 4.6 How to protect privacy during contacts).
If someone from outside your intervention team calls asking about a service user, tell them that as part of a health programme, you cannot give out information (see section 4.6 How to protect privacy during contacts).

3.2.3 Show empathy and concern
It is important that service users feel heard (validated and acknowledged), so be sure to show empathy and concern. At the same time, remember that it is not your role to solve people's problems. You are there to listen to them, help them learn and apply self-help skills, and to connect them to other sources of support when needed.
Examples of statements you might use to show empathy and concern include:
- "That sounds like it was very upsetting / challenging / frightening."
- "You have experienced many difficulties."
- "You have been through a lot."
- "Thank you for telling me that. It sounds like you have a lot of problems in your life right now and it's not surprising that you feel this way."
These statements do not need to be used word for word. Rather, they show the general type of thing that can be said, and probably need adapting to your context.

3.2.4 Acknowledge emotions
When working with people experiencing high levels of distress, it is important to acknowledge their feelings. You can do this by suggesting the emotion they might be experiencing. For example:
- "It is very sad that this has happened to you."
- "I can see that this is probably frustrating for you."
- "I can see your situation is very painful / stressful / upsetting."
- "You have many worries, but you are trying your best."
As much as possible, try not to say, "I understand how you feel / I know how you feel." This might feel dismissive and could cause a negative reaction, such as, "How can you possibly know how I feel?!"
Instead, you can use phrases such as "I can see this is probably (upsetting / difficult) for you," or "This seems really hard for you." These statements show empathy but do not suggest that you know how the person is feeling.

3.2.5 Put aside personal values
You must respect the personal values and beliefs of the people you are helping, even if you do not agree with them. Refrain from judging people who may appear to be doing little to help themselves, as they may not have the skills or resources. Working to put aside personal beliefs or values is important because it helps you interact with people in a neutral way.

3.2.6 Avoid giving advice
As a helper, you should not give advice to service users or tell them what to do if they speak to you about a problem. Giving advice means telling someone what they should or should not do. This is different from offering several suggestions to choose from, sharing options that have been useful for other people, or connecting someone with an organization for extra support.
All helpers will feel tempted to give advice sometimes. This is very common. For example, it might be very tempting when a person is reporting signs of stress or depression to tell them what you think they should do (for example, "You should talk to your partner about this").
It is important to avoid giving advice. Instead, follow the steps in our troubleshooting guide, which outlines how to help the person use their own coping strategies (see Annex 2. Troubleshooting templates).

3.2.7 Practise self-care and attend supervision
All helpers should take care of themselves, so they remain able to take care of others. Supporting people who are distressed or unwell can increase your own stress. You may hear about traumatic events - such as injury, violence or loss - which can be distressing. Other common causes of helper stress include life problems, the emotional nature of the work, feeling a sense of responsibility for service users' well-being, feeling unable to help someone, or work-related frustrations (such as people dropping out, low engagement, people not responding).
Here are some suggestions to manage your own stress.
- Regularly practise exercises from the self-help intervention (these are designed to help people manage stress).
- Think about what helped you cope with difficulties in the past.
- Take time to eat, rest and relax, even for short periods.
- Get adequate sleep and exercise.
- Keep reasonable working hours.
- Minimize your intake of alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, and avoid non-prescription drugs.
- Use supervision to discuss difficult issues that come up.
- Ask for support from, and give support to, your fellow helpers.
- Connect with friends, loved ones or other trusted people.
- Remember that not everyone will improve or be able or motivated to engage fully. Raise issues in supervision to find out if there is anything more you can do to help the person.
- Reflect on the positive experiences you had in your helper role that week and give yourself credit for your efforts and the good job you are doing. Remember that by doing your work, you are helping many people in distress.

4. How to provide support to service users
This section outlines the overall model for providing guided self-help (Figure 4.1 Overall model for contacting and supporting service users). Your organization may adapt this to your local context. It outlines the types of support contacts provided (which can be adapted for in-person delivery). If you are delivering Step-by-Step or Doing What Matters In Times of Stress, then these contacts are supplemented by the information in Chapters 5 and 6 respectively.
The aim of these contacts is to keep them to 15 minutes. Although this may seem brief for supporting someone in a psychological intervention, both research trials and real-world use of SbS and DWM have shown that effective and meaningful support can be delivered in this time. Keeping sessions short allows human resources to be used more efficiently, enabling more people to access help.
Once a person has signed up and been included in the intervention, they will be assigned to a helper. After this, you will make:

text:
4. How to provide support to service users
- A welcome contact to introduce the person to the intervention and to introduce yourself as their helper if they are receiving guidance (see section 4.1 Welcome contact). You will provide the person with more details about the intervention and answer any questions or concerns they might have.
- Regular support contacts (typically once a week) over several weeks (for example, five calls for DWM and SbS corresponding to the five sections or chapters in each intervention). Each contact follows the same format (see section 4.2 Regular support contacts). During these contacts, there are specific steps to follow if you identify a safety concern, if someone needs extra support with coping, or if other challenges arise (see sections 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns? and 4.9 How do I deal with other challenges?). If delivering Step-by-Step or Doing What Matters In Times of Stress, you will also refer to the specific information in chapters 5 and 6 during these calls.
- End contact when the person finishes the intervention to evaluate effects and outcomes and to identify and address any remaining support needs (see section 4.3 End contact). This can be combined with the last regular support contact.
Figure 4.1 Overall model for contacting and supporting service users (see relevant sections for more detail)

<!-- image -->

4.2 Regular support contacts
After the welcome contact, the service user starts the intervention. At this point you will begin to have regular (for example weekly) support contacts with them (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact for a summary of tasks for regular support contacts and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact for an example script and text). These typically last for as long as it takes for the person to complete the intervention, for example, five regular support contacts for SbS and DWM, which correspond to the five modules in the intervention (your organization should tell you the procedure for dealing with missed appointments and extending the time frame for providing support - see section 4.5 How to deal with unsuccessful contacts).
The aim of regular support contacts is to offer support and to troubleshoot any problems people have with the intervention. Between the welcome contact and the first support contact, the person should have worked through the first module.
During your regular support contacts you will (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact for a more detailed summary of tasks for regular support contacts):
- give an agenda for the support contact and remind them how long the call will last;
- ask the person how they are doing, and briefly discuss any issues they might mention;
- praise them for starting or finishing a module of the intervention;
- review the last module of the self-help intervention;*
- review the person's practice of the exercises;*
- discuss the benefits and purpose of the exercise;*
- ask them if they have any further questions or issues to raise; and
- remind them of the day and time for the next contact.
* See SbS and DWM specific information that can be added in Chapter 5 and Chapter 6.

4.2 Regular support contacts
It is important to follow the structure of the calls, but even more important to make sure that people feel validated, heard and listened to by using your basic helping skills. It can take some time to get used to doing this, especially if there is a person who is facing many problems. This will be covered in your training and can also be addressed in supervision. The aim is to complete most calls in 15 minutes, unless there are important issues to address such as a safety concern. Experience shows that with practice this can be achieved.

Extra support
During your regular support contacts, there may be times when you will be required to provide extra support. The service user may disclose information that makes you think they may be experiencing a mental disorder that might require specialized support (such as psychosis); a substance-related issue; an immediate safety concern, such as imminent risk of suicide; or an experience of sexual violence or intimate partner violence (see section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns?).
In all these situations it is important to contact your supervisor. They can advise you on the next steps. It may be that the person will benefit from extra support beyond the scope of the guided selfhelp intervention.
If there is no immediate health or safety concern but the person is distressed during your regular contacts or other challenges arise, you will need to support them to cope or troubleshoot in other ways (see section 4.9 How do I deal with other challenges?).

4.3 End contact
After the service user has finished the intervention you will have an "end contact" with them. The end contact can be integrated into the last regular support contact, or it can be scheduled as a separate contact. During the end contact, you should congratulate the service user on completing the intervention and remind them that even though they have finished, they can continue to practise the skills they have learnt.
The main aim of the end contact is to evaluate the intervention's impact and see if people need more support. Repeating the baseline measures allows a comparison of symptoms before and after the intervention. It is also helpful to collect feedback on how people experienced the intervention by conducting a satisfaction questionnaire.
Questionnaires to evaluate the intervention's impact can be made available on digital platforms, if used. You only need to remind people to complete them online. If the questionnaire identifies a need for extra support consult your supervisor. Your organization will inform you if there are any more follow-up steps to take to discharge people from the service.

4.4 Ad hoc contact
Self-help interventions are not usually a crisis or on-demand service. Your organization should give you instructions on how to deal with contacts outside usual support contact times. You should inform service users of the procedure for this at the welcome contact but you may also need to remind them of it during the intervention if they contact you outside their appointment time.
If using messages instead of calls, it is important that the service user knows your process for responding to messages, for example, that you will not read messages until the appointment time and you may not check voicemails regularly. Your organization should have clear rules and guidelines that you can explain to people, including what they should do in an emergency (such as imminent risk of suicide).

4.5 How to deal with unsuccessful contacts
If the service user does not answer the telephone or reply to your message within the agreed time frame (usually one week), you can record an unsuccessful contact attempt.
The procedure for unsuccessful contacts or "missed appointments" may differ across organizations so always check your own organization's policy before proceeding (see Box 4.1 Example policy for unsuccessful contacts for an example policy based on the approach used in SbS trials in Lebanon). To manage caseloads, organizations may wish to reduce the threshold for unsuccessful contacts from three to a lower number. See Annex 1E. Summary of tasks for end contact for example text in case people stop responding.

text:
Box 4.1 Example policy for unsuccessful contacts
If a service user cannot be reached for the appointment (for example, they do not answer their telephone or respond to a message by an agreed time point), the helper should:
- document the event as an unsuccessful contact in the case notes (see Annex 5C. Example case note for missed contact);
- send the service user a message to acknowledge the missed appointment and explain next steps;
- contact them at the usual time next week (unless they get in touch to say they want to end the intervention).
After three unsuccessful contacts, the helper should inform the programme coordinator, who will discharge the service user from the helper's caseload.
If the helper is concerned about the service user's safety, they should always liaise with their supervisor before proceeding.

text:
4.6.1 Protecting privacy in telephone or video contacts
Be aware that some people share phones, so it may not always be the service user who answers your call. It is important to ask about this in the welcome contact and to discuss what information you can share if someone else answers the phone. Your organization should have clear guidance on this issue (see Box 4.2 for an example protocol).
Never give out information about a service user or the intervention over the phone to anyone unless the service user has given you clear permission. See Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention for what to do when a service user's friend or family member is trying to get information from you.

text:
Box 4.2 Example protocol for helpers for instances when someone other than the service user answers a contact call
- Say your name and that you are calling to speak to the service user.
- If the person on the phone asks who you are, do not give confidential information about the intervention or the service. Instead, say something generic - for example, you are calling from the outreach programme of your organization.
- If the person asks further questions, you could tell them that you are doing some health promotion outreach and that you need to speak to the service user directly.
- If the person does not let you speak to the service user, say you will call again another time, and explain this is due to the organization's confidentiality policy.
- Thank them and say goodbye.
Note. Protocols for dealing with other people answering a call will depend on your country and location, so check what your organization's policy is and agree what to do in advance with your supervisor.

4.6.2 Protecting privacy in written messages
When contacting people using written messages, use the messaging platform agreed by your organization. To ensure data protection and privacy, do not use your personal email or other messaging platform to contact people.

4.7 How do I write support messages?
If you are supporting service users through written messages, take care when drafting your text. For example, you will want to make sure your messages are clear and easy to digest.
If you are providing delayed (asynchronous) support, use short sentences and paragraphs for each topic you want to address.
If you are providing live (synchronous) support, remember that the person you are talking to will be waiting for a reply and reading long pieces of text can slow down the conversation. Break your text into smaller chunks so the person can start to read while you are typing the next section. Be sure to discuss in your welcome contact how you will indicate when you are still writing (for example, write "…" at the end of your sentence) so that the service user does not reply before you finish, as this can confuse the conversation and take it off course.
Make sure your feedback is neither too long nor too short. There are no specific guidelines on the right length, as it depends on the module being covered and the service user's responses. It is important to stick to your allocated time where possible, and to ensure that the person can tell you paid attention to how they have engaged with the intervention that week. Table 4.1 Helpful dos and don'ts for writing support messages lists some other helpful dos and don'ts for writing support messages. Note that what is and is not appropriate will vary depending on local context and culture, so make sure you adapt the dos and don'ts accordingly.

4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns?
Immediate safety concerns include:
- imminent risk of suicide or self-harm;
- risk of harm to the service user or another person (for example, if the service user or someone else is experiencing physical or sexual violence, or if there is a child protection issue); and
- anything else your organization identifies as a potential safety concern.
This section presents a potential procedure for identifying and responding to safety concerns (Figure 4.2 Overall procedure for dealing with safety concerns). Please check with your organization, as they may have their own procedure that has been adapted for your context. For example, they may require you to get the service user's contact information and location in case emergency services need to be sent to support them. In all cases you should follow your organization's procedures and guidelines for identifying and addressing safety concerns.

The list of warning signs in Table 4.2 is not exhaustive, and there may also be other, culturally specific warning signs. It is important that helpers and organizations delivering guided self-help are supported by relevant professionals (such as mental health professionals) who can oversee and give guidance on safety procedures.

4.8.2 Use basic helping skills
Step 2 in the procedure for dealing with safety concerns is to use your basic helping skills to remind the service user about confidentiality, learn more about their situation and build trust.
Listen empathetically and non-judgementally, and validate the person's experience. For example:
"I'm glad you're sharing these things with me. Before we speak more, I want you to understand that everything you tell me will be kept private, unless you or someone else is in immediate danger. That means that I will not talk with your family or other people outside the [add name] team about what you have said, without your permission. But if I am very concerned that you or someone else is in immediate danger, my supervisor and I may need to speak with people outside the [add name] team to get you the best kind of help and ensure the safety of the people involved. This is because my role is to care about your welfare and safety."
Adapt this example text according to the procedures of your organization and any national guidelines.
To learn more about the person's situation and build trust, you could ask questions such as:
- "Can you tell me a bit more about the situation?"
- "What has happened to make you feel this way?"
- "How is this situation affecting you?"
- "What do you mean by that?"
Depending on the situation, you may need to assess imminent risk of suicide. Your organization should have a protocol for you to follow (see Annex 3A. Example protocol for assessing imminent risk of suicide for an example of what that might look like). If you have to ask about suicide and selfharm, make your questions clear and direct (Box 4.3 How to ask about suicide and self-harm).

text:
Box 4.3 How to ask about suicide and self-harm
- When asking about suicide and self-harm, ask direct, clear questions. Avoid using vague or evasive words that could be misunderstood.
- Direct questions help the person feel that they are not being judged for having thoughts or plans of suicide or for having made suicide attempts or self-harmed in the past.
- Some people may feel uncomfortable talking with you about suicide, but you can tell them that it is very important for you to clearly understand their level of safety.
- Asking questions about suicide will not cause the person to take action to end their life, but rather often helps them to feel understood and less distressed.
- See Annex 3A. Example protocol for assessing imminent risk of suicide for more information on asking about suicide.
If you are providing support remotely, your organization should have clear processes for you to follow if, for example, someone hangs up on you or you lose the connection when you are talking with them.
Here are some things you might do to address the challenges of working remotely (47).
- If possible, try to find out where the person is located for the support contacts, so you can identify nearby places if the person you are speaking with needs emergency assistance or referral for additional support.
- Communicate the risk protocol clearly in the first contact.
- Create a safety plan in the first remote support contact.
- Establish a backup plan at the beginning of the intervention for what to do if you get disconnected.
- If you lose contact, try reconnecting with the person. Remind them that it is important for you to ensure their safety and check whether they wish to continue with the intervention. If they do not answer and you are concerned for their safety, you may need to speak with the safety contact agreed at the start of the programme (if your organization's safety protocol includes safety contacts).
- Tell the person about different support services available, so they have options.
- Contact your supervisor to let them know you lost connection with someone with a safety concern.

4.8.3 Respond appropriately
The last step in dealing with safety concerns is to respond appropriately. This means following your organization's procedures, so make sure you know what these are.
If there are indications of imminent risk of suicide or any other immediate safety concern you must inform your supervisor immediately (Box 4.4 How to respond to someone at imminent risk of suicide). This is essential to ensure that you get the support you need to deal with the situation and that appropriate actions are taken to support the person at risk.

text:
Box 4.4 How to respond to someone at imminent risk of suicide
- Contact your supervisor immediately.
- Do not leave the person alone. Stay with them, or on the phone with them, while waiting for your supervisor or trusted person to arrive.
- Ask the person if you can contact someone they trust in the community to provide support and help to ensure that they are kept safe.
- Ask the person if they have access to any means of self-harm. Discuss ways to remove these items from their home environment.
- Attend to the person's mental state and emotional distress.
- Explore reasons and ways to stay alive.
- Focus on the person's strengths by encouraging them to talk about how earlier problems have been resolved.
- Be aware of your own response to this topic and try to follow the protocols.
If there is no indication of a safety concern, continue to support the person through your regular support contacts (see section 4.2 Regular support contacts).
Your organization should provide information about how to report an imminent risk of suicide in contexts where it is illegal. For more information on ensuring confidentiality and understanding mandatory reporting see the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Minimum Service Package (48).
Remember, one of your roles as a helper is to ensure that service users can access appropriate support and that they are kept safe.

5.2 Step-by-Step skills, modules and support contacts
SbS seeks to boost a person's activity to create pleasant emotions, a sense of achievement and connection with others to improve mood (called behavioural activation). It comprises five weekly modules and an introductory module, each focused on a specific skill (Figure 5.1 Overview of SbS modules and Table 5.1 Overview of SbS skills and exercises). Each module is divided into parts with different sections and takes around 30 minutes to complete.
All modules include exercises that people are asked to practise in their own time. In the version of SbS that was evaluated in research there was one week between modules. In that time the person was expected to complete all the content and also have time to practise. There is some flexibility to this; for example, if someone does not complete a module one week or needs longer, then support contacts can be rearranged. In the research, one welcome call and five support contacts were delivered over a maximum eight-week period to account for any delays.
Ideally, service users will practise and use all skills, but this may not happen. Instead, people may be naturally inclined to use some skills more than others. Helpers should reinforce the importance of trying all the skills, particularly stress management and taking steps to improve mood by doing activities, including social activities.

text:
Table 5.1 Overview of SbS skills and exercises
The ideal frequency for practising the different skills in SbS will differ for each service user, depending on the severity of their symptoms. The aim of the behavioural activation skills (small activities, breaking activities down and social activities) is to re-engage people in daily life. The goal is to gradually increase activity levels as the course progresses. For someone with severe depression, even doing one new activity a week, or a very small activity every day (such as a short walk), may be the most they can achieve. But for people with milder problems, it will be possible to encourage daily small activities or bigger activities a few times a week. It is important for people to pay attention to how they feel after each activity and to recognize any improvements in mood, even if they are brief.
The other skills are more aimed at reducing stress and should be practised every day after they are introduced. Some, like the grounding and breathing exercises, need repeating for people to notice their benefit. Individuals may prefer to use only grounding or breathing. Once people feel they have mastered the skill, they can use it any time they need to reduce stress.
The rest of this chapter summarizes the content of each module and gives tips for helpers to use in support calls. This should be used alongside the scripts and example texts in Annex 1. Summary of tasks for different contacts, and example scripts and texts.
Whether or not you use the example scripts or text, always remember to personalize content for each service user. It is important to look at the person's progress, address any questions they may have, and tailor your message accordingly. It is also helpful to look at the content and guidance section for the module the person has just completed before you write your reply (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact for more information).

5.2.1 Overview of support contacts for SbS
The following approach can be used when delivering SbS with support contacts (see Figure 5.1 Overview of SbS modules). Scripts are available in the annexes for live contacts and example text for messages for delayed contacts.
1. Welcome contact. See section 4.1 Welcome contact for general information on the welcome contact. In SbS, the welcome contact can be combined with additional information to support the module "Introduction: take the first steps" (see section 5.2.2 Introduction: take the first steps). See Annex 1A. Summary of tasks for welcome contact for a summary of tasks for the welcome contact and Annex 1B. Example script and text for welcome contact for an example script and text.
2. Support contacts. These are delivered weekly and are tailored to the specific SbS modules. Aim for 15 minutes per support contact.
- For general information, see Chapter 4. How to provide support to service users.
- See Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact for a summary of tasks for regular support contacts and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact for an example script or message text.
- Before each contact, review the additional information about the specific module covered in the contact and adapt sections 3 and 4 of the example script or text (Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact) (see sections below).
3. End contact. This contact can be integrated in the last support contact (module 5: "Remember, change takes time"). See section 4.3 End contact for general information, Annex 1E. Summary of tasks for end contact for a summary of tasks for the end contact and Annex 1F. Example script and text messages for end contact for an example script and text.

5.2.2 Introduction: take the first steps
The introductory module comprises three components.
- Welcome to SbS. SbS is introduced alongside an overview of what service users will learn, and how people can benefit best from the programme. The helpers are introduced, as are other parts of the intervention, such as the toolbox.
- Introduction of characters. The doctor and other characters in the story are introduced.
- Grounding. This core skill, which is practised throughout the intervention, is introduced. Service users practise three different grounding exercises: introductory, short and longer grounding (see Annex 6. Script for grounding exercise for a grounding exercise script for live contacts).

People might not yet have gone through the introductory module when you contact them.
Prepare for the call by reviewing section 4.1 for information on what to cover in this contact and Annex 1A. Summary of tasks for welcome contact and Annex 1B. Example script and text for welcome contact for a summary and example script and text.
- If people have general questions about SbS, tell them about guided self-help, the exercises they will do, and how to practise them at home.
- If someone asks about helper support, refer to the information you gave them during the welcome call and explain it again.
- If someone asks about the grounding exercise, refer to the information provided in the introduction module, and explain that it is important to practise exercises to feel their effect.
- If someone complains of light-headedness during the grounding exercises, it may be because they are breathing too deeply or too fast. You might say: "This can be a common problem. Most of the time if you feel dizzy or light-headed, it means you are breathing too fast or too deeply. Try breathing more slowly and gently."

text:
5.2.3 Module 1. Start small and reduce stress
Module 1 has four content components.
1. Psychoeducation about stress. The service user characters start sharing their story, talking about the symptoms they have experienced. The doctor character explains how experiencing adversity can lead to low mood or anxiety and physical symptoms.
2. Slow breathing exercise. Service users learn the skills of slow breathing to help reduce stress (see Annex 7. Script for slow breathing exercise for a script for slow breathing that can be used in live contacts).
3. Gratitude list. Service users are asked to think about and focus on things to be grateful for.
4. Small activities. Service users learn that what we do can have an impact on how we feel and that starting to do small activities again can help us feel better.

Psychoeducation stress
- People will probably ask about stress or might describe their symptoms to you. Use active listening and encouragement to explain that completing SbS may help them feel better.
- If someone uses medical terms such as "diagnosis", explain that people have different names for their experience (for example, distress, low mood, depression). Ask the person what term they would like to use.
This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).
- If someone asks about grounding or slow breathing, encourage them to practise these exercises regularly because we know from experience that many people find them helpful.
- If someone complains of light-headedness during breathing exercises, it may be because they are breathing too deeply or too fast. You might say: "This can be a common problem. Most of the time if you feel dizzy or light-headed, it means you are breathing too fast or too deeply. Try breathing more slowly and gently."
- If someone asks how the gratitude list will help, refer to the explanation in the module, which says that focusing on things we are grateful for helps improve how we are feeling.
- Remind people that, like all exercises, regular practice is important.

Small activities tips
- If someone asks how the small positive activities will help, you can briefly explain that our activities can affect how we feel, and that they will learn more about this in the next module.
- Praise people's efforts (no matter how small) and reiterate that it is important to practise doing enjoyable activities (people may not be used to doing this).
- Starting small is a key point here, because if people try something too big and do not manage it this early in the programme, they are at particular risk of dropping out.
- You may also spend a few minutes brainstorming ideas of enjoyable activities they could do. Try to discourage unhealthy behaviours, such as drinking alcohol and smoking.
- Help people recognize the positive changes in their mood after doing an activity. Changes may be very small, so you may need to ask questions to prompt this recognition.
- If someone has found it difficult to think about or do activities over the past week, support them to identify small activities they can schedule for next week.

5.2.4 Module 2. Break the cycle
Module 2 has four content components.
1. Story content. Story characters reflect on their experience with the small activities exercise, saying how they stopped doing pleasant activities because of low mood, and how this made them feel even worse. The doctor character explains it is usual to struggle with activities.
2. Sadness and withdrawal cycle. In the story, the doctor character explains the sadness and withdrawal cycle, which is the main therapeutic concept used in SbS. This is a vicious cycle in which a person with low mood has little energy to do anything; they withdraw and so get even more low. This vicious cycle can be broken by starting to do enjoyable activities again (behavioural activation).
3. Mood Tracker. Service users get introduced to the Mood Tracker, a tool to track their mood and help identify what makes them feel better or worse.
4. Breaking activities down. Service users learn a technique for dealing with overwhelming activities by breaking them into smaller steps so that they become more manageable.

text:
Tips on sadness and withdrawal cycle
- If someone asks about the sadness and withdrawal cycle, consider explaining it once more, emphasizing how it keeps you feeling low or sad with no energy. Remind them that wanting to withdraw is common.
- Ask about their experiences with their activities, comparing how they feel after doing the activities with how they feel not doing them, that is, how they felt before starting SbS.
- If someone did not manage to do their activities, help them identify possible causes and encourage them to try again, as it can take some time to break the cycle of feeling down.
- If someone mentions a lot of negative thoughts about themselves, acknowledge this and say we often criticize ourselves when we feel down.
- If they say they are struggling, show empathy, tell them that it is okay to struggle - many people do - and remind them that it is important to keep trying to practise the exercises. If someone says the story is overly negative, praise them for not struggling that much.
This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).

Mood Tracker
- If someone needs more information about the use of the Mood Tracker explain: "the Mood Tracker allows you to enter how you feel whenever you want to. This is helpful because tracking your mood could help you spot the things that are making you feel good or bad, and in turn do more or less of them to feel better. Tracking your mood can make it easier for you to help yourself get out of the sadness and withdrawal cycle and become more aware of your emotional state, so I really encourage you to use it."

Breaking activities down
- If someone says they feel worried about trying a bigger activity (now or during later modules), acknowledge their feelings, perhaps reflecting on how the sadness and withdrawal cycle can make us not believe in ourselves and feel very tired. Give hope and praise for taking on a larger activity.
- If someone is struggling with all the different exercises, give them any needed technical support and say that it is important to start small. Remind them that if they feel worried, it is okay to go back to the small activities exercise, or to only plan one or two steps of a challenging activity.

5.2.5 Module 3. Be kind to yourself
Module 3 has three content components.
1. Story content. In the story, characters tell how they have struggled and did not feel SbS was helping them at first. The doctor explains that this often happens, and that it is important to keep practising. Then the characters describe how they struggled with meeting their friends and how the doctor helped them with a grounding exercise and a positive self-talk exercise.
2. Positive self-talk. Service users learn how being kind to ourselves gives us more energy to cope with stressful situations.
3. Breaking activities down: problems and solutions. Service users write down potential difficulties they might face when trying to implement their scheduled activities, and ideas for overcoming them.

Breaking activities down: problems and solutions
- By this time in the programme, people may be struggling with finding new things to do, so you may need to brainstorm more ideas with them by asking them a few questions about their community and what activities are possible there. You could also give examples of what other people might have tried.
- People may find it easy to list potential difficulties but harder to identify ways of overcoming them. Check people's responses to this exercise to make sure they have identified possible solutions and not only listed problems. If they have not identified solutions, tell them that you would like to help them.

5.2.6 Module 4. Connect with others
Module 4 has three components.
1. Story content. In the story, the characters tell how they met their friends and how they felt hesitant at first but then felt relaxed and comfortable. They also share how they asked friends for support. The doctor character explains that seeing others generally helps us to feel better and that it is important to ask for help from others or organizations when you need it.
2. Social activities. Service users plan a social activity.
3. Asking for support. Service users are encouraged to ask for support.

Social activities
- If someone says they have not really stopped seeing people, explore whether they are enjoying the time they spend with others and whether it is quality time. If not, explain that planning an activity with someone you trust may still lift your mood.
- If someone didn't manage a social activity, help them identify possible causes and help them to plan one, even if it is something small.
- If someone did manage a social activity, ask them about how it made them feel (and focus on reflecting positive elements of their response). Was it fun or a challenge? What social activity might they do next time?
- If someone says they found it difficult, help them identify support and coping strategies, and explain that these can be added to their social activities exercise.
- If someone says they don't have anyone they can contact, try exploring whether they can think of someone they can reconnect with again, or someone they have just met they could get in contact with more.

Asking for help
- If someone asks you about local organizations that could help them, find out what area they live in and what they need help with. Remember to show empathy when someone is sharing their problems. Refer them to the list of services you were given by your organization.

5.2.7 Module 5. Remember, change takes time
Module 5 has two main components.
1. Story content. In the story, characters talk about how they are doing after SbS. They say how they felt better and how a difficult life event made them feel worse again. They say that they overcame the situation using the techniques they had learnt in SbS. The doctor character explains that it is common to have ups and downs, and that it is good to know our own warning signs.
2. Warning signs and coping mechanisms. Service users learn how to identify when their mood is getting worse (warning signs) and what to do if that happens (coping techniques) as a form of relapse prevention.

- Ask the person if they know what their warning signs are. If they do, encourage them to continue using the SbS techniques, especially if they notice the warning signs returning.
- If the person has not identified their warning signs, refer them back to module 5 and ask them to complete the warning signs exercise, or complete this exercise with them.
- It is really important to make a plan for the future so you can continue to maintain all the great work you have done so far. You can look out for any warning signs and put in place strategies that you know can help you.

text:
6. Information for helpers delivering Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM)
This chapter is for organizations delivering Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM). DWM is available in book form here. It can be adapted to run on a digital platform (such as https://dwmatters.eu).
This chapter contains specific information for helpers delivering DWM. It should be used alongside Chapter 4, which covers the information on the different types of contact and general information important when providing support.
Note for programme managers. Please adapt the information in this chapter to your context before sharing it with helpers.

6.1 Overview
What follows is a description of the approach used with the web application (https://dwmatters. eu), whereby a weekly support contact corresponding to each module was provided. This online version of DWM uses the same content as the book, including the same audio exercises and tool summaries. It can be accessed through a common web browser (such as Firefox, Google Chrome or Safari).
People who receive a web version of DWM need a compatible device (smartphone, tablet or computer) and a reliable internet connection (the intervention is not available offline). They may also need headphones to listen to the audio exercises.
This model of support contacts can be used with the book version and can also be adapted to fewer contacts, which may be more suitable for delivery in primary care. An adapted shorter model, which has been tested in research studies, includes three support contacts: a first welcome contact, a follow-up contact a week or two later to check progress and provide motivation and support, and a final contact a few weeks later.

6.2 DWM skills, modules and support contacts
DWM aims to teach people skills to manage stress. It comprises five weekly modules, each focused on a specific skill (Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules and Table 6.1 Overview of DWM skills and exercises). In the online version, each module (which corresponds to a chapter of the book) is divided into three submodules and includes guided exercises to help service users learn key stress management skills.
8 Contact psych\_interventions@who.int for more information.

Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules
<!-- image -->
- b The end contact can be combined with support contact 5 or delivered separately.
Table 6.1 Overview of DWM skills and exercises

| Skill | Summary | How to practise | Benefits of practice |
| - | - | - | - |
| Awareness exercise (Module 1) | The awareness exercise is sometimes called "paying attention with curiosity", which means paying full attention to whatever is happening right in front of us, without judging it as good or bad. | 1. Use your five senses to focus your full attention on an activity you are doing (such as eating, walking, cooking, cleaning, or talking or listening to someone). 2. Notice with curiosity what you can see, hear, touch, smell and taste. | · Paying attention with curiosity often helps us to focus on what we are doing and to do it better. · It can also help us to enjoy or appreciate what we are doing. |
| Grounding (Module 1) | Grounding brings us back to the present moment and unhooks us when we're caught up in emotional storms (stress). | Steps for grounding: 1. Notice your thoughts and feelings. 2. Slow down and connect with your body by stretching, pushing your feet down and focusing on your breathing. 3. Refocus on the world around you and on what you are doing. | · When we are caught up in emotional storms (causing stress) and hooked by difficult thoughts and feelings, it is hard to do anything useful. Grounding can help us to refocus on what we need to do in a stressful situation. · Practising regularly, even when we are not very stressed, can help us to then use grounding in more difficult situations. |

Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules
| Skill | Summary | How to practise | Benefits of practice |
| - | - | - | - |
| Unhooking (Module 2) | Like grounding, unhooking helps us to unhook from difficult thoughts and feelings. It is faster than grounding and can be done in just a few seconds. | 1. Notice a thought or feeling with curiosity. 2. Name the thought or feeling. 3. Refocus on the world around you and on what you are doing. | · Unhooking from difficult thoughts and feelings allows us to see them for what they are and reduces their control over our actions. · Like grounding, unhooking can help us to refocus on what we need to do and to act on our values. |
| Acting on your values (Module 3) | Acting on our values means acting in line with our deepest desires for how we want to behave as human beings, what is important to us, what kind of person we want to be, and how we want to treat others. | 1. Choose the values that are most important to you (such as being kind, being supportive, being hard working). Only you can choose which values are most important to you; no one else can decide for you. 2. Pick one small action that would be in line with your values. This could be something you do, or something you say to someone. | · Acting on our values can give us a sense of purpose and meaning, even in stressful situations. |

Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules
| Skill | Summary | How to practise | Benefits of practice |
| - | - | - | - |
| Values-guided problem solving (Module 3) | There are three approaches to any difficult situation: 1. leave; 2. change what can be changed, accept the pain that cannot be changed, and live by our values; 3. give up, lose touch with our values, and do things that do not help or make the situation worse. Values-guided problem solving focuses on option 2. | 1. Change what can be changed. Use your arms and legs and hands and feet and mouth to take action. Do whatever you can to improve your situation, no matter how small it might be. 2. Accept what cannot be changed. Use unhooking and grounding techniques to manage difficult thoughts and feelings. 3. Find other ways to live according to your values. | · Values-guided problem solving can empower us to take effective action in difficult and stressful situations. |
| Being kind (Module 4) | Being kind means using kind words and actions with ourselves and with other people. | 1. Unhook from unkind thoughts and feelings by noticing and naming them. 2. Speak to yourself kindly. You could also imagine filling one of your hands with kindness and placing it somewhere on your body where you feel pain. 3. Speak to others kindly and engage in kind actions. | · Being kind to ourselves gives us more energy to cope with stressful situations and to help others. · Being kind to others can make a difference, even in very difficult situations. It can also give us a sense of connection, well-being and fulfilment. |

Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules
| Skill | Summary | How to practise | Benefits of practice |
| - | - | - | - |
| Making room (Module 5) | Making room means allowing painful thoughts and feelings to come and go like the weather, instead of spending energy fighting them. | 1. Notice a difficult thought or feeling with curiosity. 2. Name the thought or feeling. 3. Allow painful thoughts or feelings to come and go, like the weather. Breathe into and around the feeling to make room for it. | · If we stop fighting with our thoughts and feelings and allow them to move through us, we will have more time and energy to act on our values. |
The rest of this chapter provides an overview of the content in each DWM module and gives tips for helpers on how to support service users, through example answers to likely questions. In all cases, make sure you personalize the content to each service user.

6.2.1 Contacts overview for DWM
The following approach can be used when delivering DWM with support contacts (see Figure 6.1 Overview of DWM modules).
1. Welcome contact. See section 4.1 for general information on the welcome contact. See Annex 1A. Summary of tasks for welcome contact for a summary of tasks for the welcome contact and Annex 1B. Example script and text for welcome contact for an example script and text.
2. Support contacts. these are delivered weekly and are tailored to the specific DWM modules. Aim for 15 minutes per support contact.
- For general information, see Chapter 4. How to provide support to service users.
- See Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact for a summary of tasks for regular support contacts and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact for an example script or message text.
- Before each contact, review the additional information about the specific module covered in the contact and adapt sections 3 and 4 of the example script or text (Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact) (see sections below).
3. End contact. This contact can be integrated in the last support contact (module 5, "Making room"). See section 4.3 End contact for general information, Annex 1E. Summary of tasks for end contact for a summary of tasks for the end contact and Annex 1F. Example script and text messages for end contact for an example script and text.

6.2.2 Module 1. Grounding
Module 1 includes several components.
1. Welcome to DWM and introduction. DWM is introduced and service users are asked to write down why they are using DWM and what they hope to achieve by the end of it.
2. Stress and becoming "hooked". Service users learn what stress is, and how stressful thoughts and feelings can "hook" us and create more stress.
3. Awareness exercise. Service users do an awareness exercise to learn how to pay close attention to an everyday experience, such as having a drink.
4. Grounding. Service users are introduced to the idea of grounding using the analogy of a storm to describe stress and emotions: it is best to be on the ground, where it is stable during a storm.
They practise three different grounding exercises: introductory, short and longer grounding (see Annex 6. Script for grounding exercise for a grounding script for live contacts).
5. Commitment to practice. Service users plan to practise skills learnt in the module at home.

Getting hooked
If someone asks what getting "hooked" means, say:
"Getting 'hooked' means that a difficult thought or feeling has taken your attention away from what you are doing. For example, you are talking with your friends, then you start thinking about something stressful. This 'hooks' you: you get lost in your thoughts and cannot focus on talking with your friends any more."
This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).

Awareness exercise
If someone asks about the awareness of drinking exercise, say:
"The aim of this exercise is to experience giving all your attention to the activity you are doing, in this case drinking. This is very different from how we normally drink without paying much attention to it. Learning to give something our full attention is the first step towards learning to manage stress better."

Grounding
If someone asks about grounding, explain:
"Grounding is a technique for managing emotional storms and intense emotional states. In such moments, we can get lost in what we are thinking and how we are feeling and lose connection with what we are doing. Grounding brings us back to the present moment by using our senses."
"With grounding, we are not trying to get rid of our difficult thoughts and feelings. Rather, we are just trying to unhook ourselves from them, and to connect with the world around us while they pass."
If people think they are not doing the grounding exercise right, explain:
"The purpose of grounding is to connect with whatever is happening in the present.
Notice your thoughts and feelings. Slow down and connect with your body by stretching, pushing your feet down, and focusing on your breathing. Refocus on the world around you and on what you are doing.
It is common to get distracted and it does not mean you are doing anything wrong."
If the exercise makes someone feel uncomfortable, say:
"That is okay, you can skip any parts that are uncomfortable."
If someone says they get dizzy or light-headed during grounding, it may be because they are breathing too deeply or too fast. Say:
"This can be a common problem. Most of the time If you feel dizzy or light-headed, it means you are breathing too fast or too deeply. Try breathing more slowly and gently."

6.2.3 Module 2. Unhooking
Module 2 includes six components.
1. Introduction. Service users are welcomed back and encouraged to continue practising the awareness and grounding exercises.
2. Summary of last week. Service users review the concept of getting hooked by difficult thoughts and feelings.
3. Difficult thoughts and feelings. Service users are given an overview of the different ways that people use to try to get rid of difficult thoughts and feelings, noting how these generally do not work. A new approach to unhooking from them is then introduced.
4. Notice and name. Service users are encouraged to identify and write down or draw the types of thoughts and feelings they have in their body that hook them.
5. Refocus. Service users are instructed how to refocus (the third and final step in unhooking) by fully engaging in an activity and giving their full attention to whoever they are with and whatever it is they are doing.
6. Recap and commitment to practice. Key points are summarized and service users plan how to practise unhooking at home.

If someone complains that they can't get rid of their thoughts and feelings, say:
"Many of us were taught from an early age that we should be able to control our thoughts and feelings. As children we might have been told to 'stop crying' or 'cheer up'. Or we might think that because we can control things in other areas of our lives (such as what we do), we should be able to control our thoughts and feelings as well. The reality is that thoughts and feelings do not work that way. We cannot control what we think or how we feel at any given moment. In fact, trying to get rid of a particular thought or feeling usually makes it more powerful."
If someone asks why it is important to learn how to notice and name difficult thoughts and feelings, explain:
"Noticing and naming difficult thoughts and feelings allows us to see them for what they are. By doing this, they have less impact and influence over us. As you become more practised at unhooking, you will find that difficult thoughts and feelings lose their ability to frighten, disturb, worry or depress you."

6.2.4 Module 3. Acting on your values
Module 3 comprises seven components.
1. Introduction. Service users briefly review concepts from module 2 and are encouraged to keep practising.
2. Values. Service users are introduced to the concept of values and how these differ from goals. They discuss how we may not be able to achieve our goals but can always find ways to act on our values. We can either act in line with our values or move away from them.
3. Identifying your values. Service users review a list of values and select those they think are most important.
4. Acting on your values. Service users are asked to think of a role model in their community, and consider what actions this person takes that they admire, and what values this person demonstrates through these actions. Then they choose which of these values they would like to model.
5. Making your action plan. Service users think of a relationship that is important to them, identify the values they want to live by in this relationship and then plan small steps that they can take to act on these values.
6. Values-guided problem solving. Service users learn how to address problems in their lives by changing what can be changed, accepting the pain of what cannot be changed, and living by their values (that is, being the sort of person they want to be).
7. Recap and commitment to practice. Key points are summarized and service users plan how to practise values-guided problem solving at home.

Tips for helpers (see also Table 6.1 Overview of DWM skills and exercises)
This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).

Values
If someone wants to understand more about values and actions, you could say:
"Our values guide our actions. A value is our deep desire for how we want to behave in life. For example, if my value is to be kind, an action might be to look after someone who is unwell. When stressed, we may act in ways that move us away from our values. But at any point, we can choose instead to say and do things that move us back towards our values."
If someone seems confused or does not understand the values exercises, say:
"The idea of values can be difficult to understand at first, but this explanation may help. When you read the list of values, which ones described the kind of person you would like to be? For example, maybe one person's values are being 'hard working' and 'responsible', while someone else's values are being 'caring' and 'loyal'. It's okay if your values are different from other people's, or if your values are different from what people say your values should be. You are the only person who can decide which values are important to you."
If someone asks why values are important, say:
"Identifying and connecting with our values gives us a sense of meaning and fulfilment. That is because no matter what our circumstances are or how difficult our lives might be, all of us can live by our values right now. We might not be able to control many things in our lives, but we can always behave like the sort of person we want to be, even in difficult situations."
"Values also give a sense of purpose to our lives. They can guide us and motivate us as we move through life. When we are guided by our values, we can unhook from our difficult thoughts and feelings more easily, and then focus on what is important to us."

Action plans
If someone cannot or does not want to write an action plan to show how they will act on their values, support and encourage them to give it a go. Give some examples of action plans (Box 6.1). You might say:
"Imagine doing one thing that is in line with your values and who you want to be as a person. Try to make a realistic plan and then imagine doing it. If you are unsure about how to do this, or would rather not do this exercise, that is okay."

text:
Box 6.1 Example action plans for acting on your values
- If I value being hard working, but I do not have a job, I could still act on my value by spending time each day looking for work, or taking care of my responsibilities such as looking after children, or helping others, even if I feel discouraged sometimes.
- If I value being kind and caring, I could act on my value by visiting my neighbour who is sick, spending some time talking to her, and making her some food.

6.2.5 Module 4. Being kind
Module 4 comprises five components.
1. Introduction. Service users are introduced to the module and encouraged to keep practising.
2. Importance of kindness. Service users consider how kindness from others is important and how we often need to learn how to be kind to ourselves.
3. Unhooking from unkind thoughts. The idea of unhooking is reviewed and service users use an audio exercise to support their practice.
4. Small acts of kindness. Service users learn how small acts of kindness can make a difference in even very difficult situations, and are asked to identify things they can say or do to be kind to others.
5. Recap and commitment to practice. Key points are summarized and service users plan how to practise small acts of kindness over the coming week.

This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).
If someone says that they already do a great deal for others, say:
"Yes, it sounds as though you are already kind and caring and do lots for people. This exercise is asking you to pay attention to the kind things that you already do, think of any additional things that you could say and do, and then to notice the effect it has on you."
If someone asks why they need to be kind to themselves, say:
"Sometimes when we really need a kind friend, no one is available. When you are kind to yourself, everyone in your life benefits. The kinder and more supportive you are to yourself, the more energy and motivation you will have to help or care for others. Similarly, when you are unkind or unfriendly to yourself, everyone in your life is worse off. Treating yourself in this harsh way saps your energy and lowers your motivation, leaving you less able to help or care for others."
If someone asks how they can practise being kind to themselves, suggest the following steps:
"First, unhook from unkind thoughts. When you catch yourself speaking to yourself in a very harsh or critical way, notice: 'Here is an unkind thought.'
Next, silently say to yourself, in a kind and caring voice, 'This hurts. This is really difficult. This is natural … Everyone has difficult thoughts and feelings like these … All people experience this when they are stressed.'
Next, try out a friendly physical gesture: put your hand over your heart, or on your belly or forehead - wherever feels soothing and comforting. Send a message to yourself with this hand: 'I see you are in pain, and I care about you, and I am here for you.' Feel the warmth and kindness flowing from your hand into your body.

6.2.6 Module 5. Making room
Module 5 comprises five components.
1. Introduction. Service users review the unhooking concept and are encouraged to keep practising.
2. Making room for pain. Service users are introduced to the concept of making room using metaphors.
3. Notice it, name it, and make room for it. Service users make room for difficult thoughts and feelings by noticing and naming them and allowing them to be present, instead of struggling to get rid of them. They practise this skill with an audio exercise.
4. Being kind to yourself. Service users do a new audio exercise, imagining their hand filling with kindness and using that hand to pour kindness into any area of their body where they feel pain.
5. What comes next. Service users are congratulated for completing DWM and are encouraged to continue practising the skills they have learnt at home. If relevant, remind people that they will be asked to fill out a questionnaire and share how they can access this.

- The support contact for module 5 of DWM has an "end contact" incorporated. See Annex 1E. Summary of tasks for end contact for a summary of tasks for the end contact and Annex 1F. Example script and text messages for end contact for an example script and text.
- If people feel sad or worried that this is the last module, encourage them to keep practising the skills they have learnt.
This information can be used for section 4, on reviewing practice of techniques and exercises, of the support contact scripts (see Annex 1C. Summary of tasks for regular support contact and Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact).
If someone asks how making room is different from trying not to think about things, say:
"This can be confusing at first, but accepting pain is different from just doing nothing or trying not to think about it. When accepting it, you acknowledge that the pain is there, you feel the pain, and then make room for it. You allow it to be there instead of pushing it away or ignoring it. An important idea here is that with time all feelings come and go if we let them just be there."
If people confuse grounding, unhooking and making room, explain:
"You might notice that this skill is similar to others you have learnt in this course. Many of the skills in this course are based on the same initial step of noticing your thoughts and feelings. Each skill does something slightly different. Grounding is for when you are wrapped up in an emotional storm. Unhooking is when you notice a difficult thought or feeling, it can be quicker than grounding. Making room is more for painful feelings. It adds another step to noticing and naming by imagining the breath flowing in and around the painful feeling. You might find you prefer some of the exercises or that they help in different situations. Try to practise all of them, but it is okay if you don't like or don't get all of them. Use whatever you feel helps you the most."

Annexes: tools and templates

Note for programme managers.
All the tools and templates in this section need adapting to align with your organization's own context and existing procedures. Please check the manual web page for information on how to access editable versions of these.
93

Note for implementing organizations
Annexes 1A-1G provide a summary of key tasks and example scripts and text for the different types of support contacts that are used when providing guided self-help. They are based on versions used in trials of SbS and DWM. They provide an overview of the different support contacts and topics to be covered. They should be adapted for local contexts and the helper's style. All information can be adapted but implementing organizations should pay particular attention to information [in square brackets]. These can also be adapted for use in person (for example, for integration in existing primary health care consultations) or for more or fewer support contacts.
When implementing SbS or DWM, the information to add to these templates can be found in Chapters 5 and 6, respectively.

Note for helpers
It is important that before the welcome contact you read any information you have been given about the service user, for example from a referring agency or through an online platform. If there is information that suggests the person has a safety concern (for example, risk of imminent suicide) you must follow your organization's risk protocol (see section 2.4.2 Addressing safety and protection concerns and Annex 3. Example protocols to assess and address safety and protection concerns). After each contact, follow your organization's procedures for recording key information about the contact, for example using case notes (see Annex 5. Case note examples).
