text:
1. Welcome the service user and introduce yourself
- Give the person your name and welcome them to the intervention.
- Tell them you are contacting them to explain more about the intervention.
- Ask them how they are (in the customary way).
- Explain how many minutes you have with them [15 minutes for SbS and DWM].
- Ask them what name they would like to be called.
- If the person is using a shared telephone for contacts, confirm who you should ask for when calling and tell the person how you will explain the reason for your call to anyone else who answers (for example, a call concerning health promotion from a local health organization). [Confirm any other phone security measures for shared telephones in line with organizational procedures].
- [Confirm the person's physical location, or the contact details for a supportive person, if applicable] who can be contacted in an emergency.

2. Tell them about the intervention
Briefly explain the intervention. Key points to make include:
- The intervention comprises [X number of modules], which are completed [X time frame e.g. weekly/over 5/6 weeks].
- If using a digital intervention, ensure that the person managed to access the platform and can navigate it.
- People using the intervention follow the materials through [X format e.g. mobile app/ online/book/video], which takes around [X minutes e.g. 30/40/50] minutes. It is good to review the content at least once a week.
- After they complete a module, people should take time to practise the skills they have learnt. This is important because the intervention works better when you practise what you have learnt between modules.
- New content will be available after [X time, e.g. all at once or unlocked on a time schedule] and the person can then move onto the next module.

text:
3[A]. (If person has chosen guidance) Explain what the service user can expect of you as their helper
Key points to make include:
- You are there to guide the person through the intervention. You are not a professional therapist and will offer support with the intervention but can only give limited help with other issues (such as financial or other problems).
- You will contact them approximately [X frequency e.g. once a week/every two weeks] for a maximum of [X time e.g. 15 minutes] because you are supporting many people each week.
- When you contact them, you will try [X number of attempts e.g. two/three/four] times according to their preferred way of contact; and if these are all unsuccessful, you will stop contacting them.
- Everything they tell you will be kept confidential, unless they or somebody else is at risk of harm. Mention how you might discuss information in supervision, but emphasize that the intervention team is also bound by the same confidentiality rules that you are. [Add any other relevant information about this in line with organizational procedures.]
- [Only if applicable] They will be asked to complete a [periodic/end of intervention/ follow-up] questionnaire, which is designed to help us know how the intervention helps people. They only have to fill it in if they want to. [Add any other relevant information about follow-up.]
- If they feel they need it, you can point them to sources of extra support, such as local support services. [Add any other relevant information about other support.]
Explain the format of future calls, telling the person that you will first cover their experiences with the modules and then with practising the activities. You will also discuss any question they have related to the modules or activities. Ask them if they have any other questions, or whether they want to add anything else before you finish. Check if they can access the intervention application.
If the person starts talking about other problems they have faced, remember this is okay. Allow them to talk and express themselves and show empathy. But try not to let this exceed five minutes before moving on.

- Ask the service user if they would like to know more about the difference between completing the intervention guided or unguided.

I am here to offer support with [intervention name] but am limited in how much I can help with other issues (such as financial problems or general questions). - I have about [15/20/etc.] minutes a week to help you and I am looking forward to working with you.

As it is a short amount of time, I will tell you when you have five minutes left for the [call/chat] so that we make best use of the time. If you want, I can send you a reminder that we have a meeting [the day before (or as agreed with the individual)].

metadata.heading_path: Preparation and follow-up tasks (or key tasks) for regular support contacts

text:
Preparation and follow-up tasks (or key tasks) for regular support contacts
- Use this summary of tasks as a checklist of everything to cover.
- Adapt the regular support example script or text (Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact) for every contact.
- Personalize the contact to each service user (that is, use their name and other previously used personal information).
- Adapt section 4 "Review activities and exercises" to the intervention and module you are covering (for example, if the contact is after module 1 of SbS, you will adapt this section to cover key aspects of SbS module 1, such as using the grounding exercise). You can find the specific information in Chapter 5 for SbS and Chapter 6 for DWM.
- Adapt the script or message to your own style.
- Before the contact, remember (if technically possible, depending on how the self-help content is accessed) to check how much of the module they completed.
- The aim is to complete contacts in 15 minutes.
- Write up a case note to document your contact (see Annex 5. Case note examples).

1. Greet the service user
- Share why you are contacting them and how long the support contact will be.

metadata.topic: 2. Ask the service user how they are this week
metadata.heading_path: 2. Ask the service user how they are this week
metadata.module: 2. Ask the service user how they are this week
metadata.section: 2. Ask the service user how they are this week

text:
2. Ask the service user how they are this week
- If the person starts talking about other problems they have faced, remember this is okay. Allow them to talk and express themselves and show empathy, but try not to let this exceed five minutes before moving on.
- If the person seems overwhelmed by their problems and are asking for your help, consider taking a few minutes to help identify support and coping strategies (see Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact and Annex 2C. Service user needs support coping).
- If someone is low in mood, they may have negative thoughts about themselves (for example, "I am weak" or "It is my fault"). Acknowledge these thoughts and beliefs and
explain that these are common when people face difficulties in life, particularly when someone experiences depression or stress. You can explain that thoughts are just thoughts, and having these thoughts does not make them true. You can refer people to useful skills in the intervention (for example, "being kind to yourself" in DWM and SbS).
If the person mentions any possible safety issues, see section 5.2.5 Module 3. Be kind to yourself.

3. Review the last module
Add specific intervention and module information to this section. For SbS and DWM, see the module content overviews in Chapters 5 and 6.
- If needed, review content from the module.
- Talk to the person about how they got on with the latest module.
- Praise them for starting or finishing the module.
- Ask them what they learnt from the module and any thoughts they had about it - did they understand the concept? If the intervention uses a story approach, can they relate to the characters?

4. Review activities and exercises
Add specific intervention and module information to this section. For SbS and DWM, see the module overviews in Chapters 5 and 6.
- Ask the person how they found the module and the techniques covered in the module, if they were able to do the activities or exercises, or what was helpful or hard.
- If necessary, remind the person of the aim of the exercise they were asked to try (see Chapters 5 and 6 for information about specific modules for SbS and DWM so you can personalize your contact to the relevant module).
In some digital self-help interventions, you may be able to use the platform to check whether the person has completed them before you have your support contact. Always let the person know that you will do this so they are aware how you got the information.
- If the person completed the activities, review this with them and ask them how they found doing the exercise. Be positive and supportive of the effort.
- If the person did not complete the activities, give them an overview of what happens in that part of the module, and discuss this with them. Consider completing the exercise with them. Have a further discussion about completing the activities. This may naturally flow from, or happen in, the section above, so may not always be needed. Otherwise, open a discussion about practising exercises in the person's own life.
- If the person managed to practise the exercises and techniques, praise them for doing so. Explore how it made them feel to do some enjoyable activities. Did it make them feel better, even if for a short while?
- If the person tells you the exercises did not go well, or they say they did not do any, normalize and try to identify barriers and how to overcome them.
- If the person could not identify any ways to overcome barriers, name some possible solutions, preferably two or more so the person has a choice.

5. Finish the contact
- Remind the person you have five minutes left (if live contact).
- Ask if they have any questions or anything they would like to discuss.
- Remind them of the day and time of the next appointment.
- Say goodbye.

Annex 1D. Example script and text for regular support contact
- See box in Annex 1C on how to use this script.
- Before every support contact, review the module-specific information in Chapters 5 and 6 and adapt the script of the message text.
- The aim is to complete contacts in 15 minutes.

1. Greeting
- "I am contacting you today to give you some support on using [intervention name]. It's a chance for us to discuss your progress and help with anything that has been difficult in using it. I have [number of minutes] to discuss this with you today."

metadata.topic: 2. Ask the service user how they are doing
metadata.heading_path: 2. Ask the service user how they are doing
metadata.module: 2. Ask the service user how they are doing
metadata.section: 2. Ask the service user how they are doing

text:
2. Ask the service user how they are doing
- "How are you doing? How have you been feeling the last week?"
If the person is in low mood or expresses negative thoughts about themselves, offer some brief support, for example by saying:
- "It sounds as though you are [low in mood/criticizing yourself]. This sometimes happens when people experience depression or feel down. It is a natural reaction to adversity. Remember that thoughts are just thoughts: just because you have them it doesn't make them true. You are not weak to experience depression and you should never blame yourself for it."
If the person is distressed or appears to need more support with coping, follow the advice in the troubleshooting guide in Annex 2. Troubleshooting templates.

3. Review the module
- (if needed). "In this week and module you were introduced to [add content from module]. Even if your story is different, remember you can still use this to help you out.
- How was it this week - have you been able to go through the module? Was there anything in particular you found helpful?
- Was there anything you didn't like about it or found confusing?
- Is there anything about any of the techniques or exercises that you'd like to clarify?"

metadata.topic: 4. Review practice of techniques and exercises
metadata.heading_path: 4. Review practice of techniques and exercises
metadata.module: 4. Review practice of techniques and exercises
metadata.section: 4. Review practice of techniques and exercises

text:
4. Review practice of techniques and exercises
If using a platform that allows you to see if module activities were completed, then adapt these questions as needed. For SbS and DWM, add module-specific information from Chapter 5 and Chapter 6.
- "How did practising the exercises at home go for you this week?
- Were you able to [name activity]?"
If the person practised the exercises:
- "It is really great that you managed to find time to use the techniques this week. How did you find the practice?"
Ask the person to share what kind of activities they are planning.
- "That's really good, I'd like to hear how they go."
If harmful coping behaviours or activities (for example, drinking alcohol to control emotions) are suggested, try to suggest more helpful alternatives.
- "Great to hear you have thought of something to do. How do you think [name activity] will help you?"
If the person did not practise the exercises:
- "It can be hard finding time to do the exercises or use the techniques. Don't worry if you weren't able to do everything you wanted to. Every little bit of practice is important. What were some of the problems that got in your way? What do you think you can do to make it more likely that you will practise the techniques more next week?
- If you couldn't think of any activities to do, maybe I could help you to think of some things.
- The idea would be to try something small that you might usually enjoy or something that would make you feel proud .Do you have any ideas of what this could be?"
Try to help the person make a plan on when they can practice.
If the person does not have any ideas on how to overcome barriers:
- "Some people I've spoken with have found that setting a time to do their activity in advance, linking it to a common activity (such as getting up or going to bed) or explaining to their family that they need some time to do the exercises helps. Would any of these be something you could try?"

Finish the call
- "We have five minutes left to talk. Do you have any questions or is there anything else you would like to say before I go?
- That's the end of our call today. I will call again next week on the [date and time]. Would you like me to send you a reminder before our next call?"

text:
Summary of tasks for end contact
1. Congratulate the service user on completing the intervention, and ask them whether they notice any difference compared with how they felt when they started SbS.
2. Remind them that even though they have finished, they can continue to practise the skills they have learnt. Help motivate people by reflecting on their positive change. Be realistic and acknowledge that sometimes our mood fluctuates, but try to also convey a positive attitude.
3. Explain if and how they can still get access to the intervention materials.
4. Remind them that it is important to complete any final questionnaires and inform them about any further follow-ups or assessments protocols (to be adapted by the implementing organization).
5. If someone does not feel better, suggest that they get help from a local service (to be provided by the implementing organization).

Live end contact script
"It is the last of our scheduled support contact today. But don't worry, because with all the skills you have learnt, I hope you will manage a little better and get more enjoyment out of life.
You made it to the end of [intervention name], that's great! I can see that you have shown real dedication and determination in finishing. I hope you enjoyed it and can see some benefits in your life compared with before you started."

text:
Annex 2A. Service user experiences distress during a contact
Anger, sadness or anxiety are normal human emotions. It is uncommon but it can happen that a service user becomes very distressed during a support contact. They may get angry, sad or worried. In some cases they may be very anxious (for example, experiencing an anxiety or panic attack where they find it hard to breathe or being anxious about a serious health problem).

text:
1. Remain calm and acknowledge the distress
Be aware of your own stress and keep your voice and breathing calm. Acknowledge the person's distress by saying what you are hearing or seeing.
- "I hear that you are feeling anxious/sad/angry at the moment …"

2. Give time and space
Allow time and space for the person to feel distressed. If they are crying you don't need to make them stop. Remain calm and supportive.
You can offer to talk to them about what is upsetting them, but do not rush into doing this. Allowing a few minutes to be distressed means they may start talking to you about it. If they do, then listen and use your helping skills.

metadata.topic: 3. Consider an exercise to reduce distress
metadata.heading_path: 3. Consider an exercise to reduce distress
metadata.module: 3. Consider an exercise to reduce distress
metadata.section: 3. Consider an exercise to reduce distress

text:
3. Consider an exercise to reduce distress
If the user is distressed, for example panicking, feeling very angry or out of control, suggest that they do a grounding exercise (see Annex 6. Script for grounding exercise) or a slow breathing exercise (see Annex 7. Script for slow breathing exercise). Remind them that you are there to help them.
- "Shall we try a breathing/grounding exercise together? I'm here to help you."

metadata.topic: 4. Remind them that emotions like this are natural
metadata.heading_path: 4. Remind them that emotions like this are natural
metadata.module: 4. Remind them that emotions like this are natural
metadata.section: 4. Remind them that emotions like this are natural

text:
4. Remind them that emotions like this are natural
- "How you're feeling is really natural, many people feel like this but these emotions and thoughts will pass.
- Emotions are there to help protect us and get us to take a helpful action.
- Unpleasant emotions are hard to bear, just know they are not there to harm us and will pass."

metadata.topic: 5. When calmer, offer to help them identify support and coping strategies.
metadata.heading_path: 5. When calmer, offer to help them identify support and coping strategies.
metadata.module: 5. When calmer, offer to help them identify support and coping strategies.
metadata.section: 5. When calmer, offer to help them identify support and coping strategies.

text:
5. When calmer, offer to help them identify support and coping strategies.
- "Would you like me to help you to think about what you could do?" and "I have a list of contact details of some local organizations that may be able to help you."
If appropriate, you may want to explore support options (see Annexes 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact and 2C. Service user needs support coping).

metadata.topic: 6. End this part of the contact and move back to the intervention
metadata.heading_path: 6. End this part of the contact and move back to the intervention
metadata.module: 6. End this part of the contact and move back to the intervention
metadata.section: 6. End this part of the contact and move back to the intervention

text:
6. End this part of the contact and move back to the intervention
Ask the service user whether they want to continue with the contact or end it at this point.
- "Shall we continue and move back to the content, or would you prefer to leave it here for today?"

7. Inform your supervisor if needed
If it is a particularly distressing situation or it has upset you, speak to your supervisor and if necessary take a bit of time before your next contact with the service user.
Be sure to inform your supervisor about what happened next time you meet if it was not an emergency.

Hi [name],
It sounds like you might be experiencing some distress. If you are, try not to worry, this is natural, especially when we go through difficult times. These feelings will pass but there might be more we can do to help you in the meantime.
I wondered if you have tried the breathing or grounding exercise from the [Step-by-Step programme/DWM] and if that helps you? Or talking to someone close to you about how you are feeling?
I also wondered if you would like to have a call to discuss how you're feeling a bit more, and I can tell you about some of your local support organizations.
Let me know if you'd like to do this, and as always remember that if you are in a crisis you can also contact the emergency services.
Kind regards,
[your name]

metadata.topic: Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact
metadata.module: Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact
metadata.section: Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact

text:
Annex 2B. Service user needs more support for other problems in their life than can be provided in a brief support contact
Some people may find it difficult to stop talking about problems in their life that cause them distress, making it hard to focus on the intervention. As a self-help intervention with only brief weekly support, the amount of time that can be provided to supporting service users with other problems in their life is limited. In a short call it is usually possible to offer some (limited) support with a problem, while also focusing on the intervention. It is important to try to do both, but this can be challenging for helpers, especially when new. This can be addressed with ongoing supervision.
Here it is important to respond using your basic helping skills, allowing the person time to talk, but also linking back to skills in the intervention that might help them or other sources of support. Try to make sure the person does not feel rushed or that the only thing they can talk about is the intervention. At the same time, try to move the conversation back to the intervention after a brief time. It may feel unusual, but signposting and support can be provided quite quickly. Remember not to become the person's therapist or social worker.

metadata.topic: 1. Use basic helping skills to provide support
metadata.heading_path: 1. Use basic helping skills to provide support
metadata.module: 1. Use basic helping skills to provide support
metadata.section: 1. Use basic helping skills to provide support

text:
1. Use basic helping skills to provide support
Do not force the person to talk but explain that you are there to provide support if desired. Sometimes just acknowledging a person's distress and simply offering to listen to them can be enough.
- "How can I help? Is there something you would like to speak to me about?
- Thank you for sharing your experiences with me. It sounds really difficult."
If the person is very distressed, you could say something like this:
- "I can see that you're very upset. I am here to support you. We can talk or just sit here quietly."

metadata.topic: 2. Identify the service user's current coping and use of intervention skills, while reminding them of your role and the limited help you can provide
metadata.heading_path: 2. Identify the service user's current coping and use of intervention skills, while reminding them of your role and the limited help you can provide
metadata.module: 2. Identify the service user's current coping and use of intervention skills, while reminding them of your role and the limited help you can provide
metadata.section: 2. Identify the service user's current coping and use of intervention skills, while reminding them of your role and the limited help you can provide

text:
2. Identify the service user's current coping and use of intervention skills, while reminding them of your role and the limited help you can provide
- "I'm not able to offer much direct help with things outside [intervention name]. But we can spend a few minutes talking together to see if there is anything that can help.
- What are you doing to cope or get support?
- Have you found any skills from the course helpful?"
If needed, encourage the person to continue using any positive and safe coping strategies.
- "This sounds like a difficult situation for you. What are you doing to cope or to get support?
- It sounds like this is helping you to cope. I would encourage you to continue with it."
You can also encourage the person to use the skills they have learnt in the intervention. If someone is very clearly distressed, you can offer to lead them through one, for example a brief grounding exercise.
- "Have you found any exercises in this course helpful?
- Do you think it could be helpful to practise [name skill] now? Or, would you like me to talk you through a grounding exercise?"

metadata.topic: 3. Signpost the service user to another service that may be able to help them
metadata.heading_path: 3. Signpost the service user to another service that may be able to help them
metadata.module: 3. Signpost the service user to another service that may be able to help them
metadata.section: 3. Signpost the service user to another service that may be able to help them

text:
3. Signpost the service user to another service that may be able to help them
Ask questions to help the person think of other ways to support themselves (for example, calling on specific people or organizations, or using new intervention skills). It is important to ask open questions and to make suggestions rather than give advice. You can suggest local organizations or resources (such as a community leader or refugee organization) for some problems that the person tells you about (such as medical conditions, requests for help with food or employment). If the person does not already know about these services and supports, encourage them to connect with them. But remember that it is the person's choice whether they follow through or not.
- "Are there other people or organizations who might help you with this?
- What have you done in the past when you have faced difficulties? Would doing that help you now?
- Some people may find that an organization or an important person, such as [the village leader], can help at times like this. Can you think of an organization or an important person who could help with this?
- Are there skills you have learnt in [intervention name] that could help with this problem?"

metadata.topic: Annex 2C. Service user needs support coping
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2C. Service user needs support coping
metadata.module: Annex 2C. Service user needs support coping
metadata.section: Annex 2C. Service user needs support coping

text:
1. Summarize and paraphrase
Summarize your understanding of the situation and remind the person that you can only offer limited help in your role as helper.
- "I see … so it sounds as though you are having trouble with [X problem]. As you know, I can only offer limited help to you, but we could speak for a few minutes to see if we can identify things that might help you."

metadata.topic: 2. Identify current supports or coping strategies the person is using that may be helpful
metadata.heading_path: 2. Identify current supports or coping strategies the person is using that may be helpful
metadata.module: 2. Identify current supports or coping strategies the person is using that may be helpful
metadata.section: 2. Identify current supports or coping strategies the person is using that may be helpful

text:
2. Identify current supports or coping strategies the person is using that may be helpful
Encourage the person to identify and use any positive and healthy coping strategies they have available. You can also encourage them to use the intervention's skills, such as slow breathing or grounding, to help them feel calmer. For example:
- "This sounds like a difficult situation for you. What are you doing to cope?
- What have you done in the past to cope with similar difficulties?
- What might you say to a friend who was going through this?
- It sounds as though [X strategy] is helping you to cope with this situation. I would encourage you to continue with it. Remember that the slow breathing and grounding exercises can be used to help you feel calmer in the moment."
If the person is doing nothing to cope you can say:
- "It sounds as though you're finding things really tough and don't know what to do to cope. Let's see if we can think of anything together that might help."

metadata.topic: 3. If needed, help the person identify additional strategies and resources for coping with their situation
metadata.heading_path: 3. If needed, help the person identify additional strategies and resources for coping with their situation
metadata.module: 3. If needed, help the person identify additional strategies and resources for coping with their situation
metadata.section: 3. If needed, help the person identify additional strategies and resources for coping with their situation

text:
3. If needed, help the person identify additional strategies and resources for coping with their situation
Ask the person if they can think of any strategies or resources they could use to help them cope - for example, people they could talk to or intervention skills they could use.
Ask if they are aware of any organizations that they can contact for support (for example, with a medical condition, financial problem or relationship issue).
If they are unsure, you could signpost them to trusted organizations (such as a community leader, refugee organizations, mental health charities, helplines), but remember to make this a suggestion rather than giving them advice.
You could say:
- "Are there other people or organizations that might help you with this?
- What have you done in the past when you faced difficulties? Would doing that help you now?
- Are there skills you have learnt in the intervention that can help with this problem?"
Encourage the person to connect with these other resources but remember that it is their decision whether they follow through with your suggestions.

4. Summarize
Repeat back what the person has said they will do to get help and gently bring the conversation back to the intervention support contact.
- "It sounds as though you're having a tough time, so to summarize, we've said that you'll try talking to your friend and contacting [name organization] for help. Let's review when we next speak and if it's okay with you, we'll continue with talking about [intervention name]?"

Example message for delayed contact
Hi [name],
It sounds as though there is a lot going on for you now. I understand that [X is happening, for example, you are concerned about your financial situation]. Unfortunately I'm only able to offer limited support with that because my role is limited to [intervention name] and it's not my expertise.
I wondered if there is anything you can try to help you - perhaps talking to a trusted loved one or a support organization? Do you know any local to you? You could try for example [X organization], who I know have helped people with this sort of thing in the past.
Even though you are worried about this, it sounds as though you have made good progress with [intervention name]. Do you have any questions about the modules so far? Let me know how you get on with the next module and I will be in touch again next week.
Kind regards, [your name]
If the external problem relates to a risk issue, such as imminent risk of suicide, or a protection concern, always follow your organization's relevant protocol (see section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns? and Annex 3. Example protocols to assess and address safety and protection concerns).

metadata.topic: Annex 2D. Service user continues to talk about the intervention beyond the agreed contact time, or sends very long messages
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2D. Service user continues to talk about the intervention beyond the agreed contact time, or sends very long messages
metadata.module: Annex 2D. Service user continues to talk about the intervention beyond the agreed contact time, or sends very long messages
metadata.section: Annex 2D. Service user continues to talk about the intervention beyond the agreed contact time, or sends very long messages

text:
Annex 2D. Service user continues to talk about the intervention beyond the agreed contact time, or sends very long messages
Service users may want to talk about the intervention or life difficulties for longer than the allocated contact time. This may be more common in earlier support contacts, when people may not be used to the idea of such a short time slot. To help to avoid this problem, remind the person about time frames:
- at the start of the contact:
- "Remember we only have [15 minutes] together today."
- towards the end of the contact:
- "We only have five minutes left to talk".
In some situations (for example, imminent risk of suicide) you may need to extend the call. If someone wants to talk beyond [15 minutes], continue being empathetic, kind and sensitive in your responses.
Follow the steps below to help end the call.

1. Stop the conversation
At the end of the [15 minutes], tell the person that you're sorry but you'll have to stop them there as you're at the end of the support contact .

2. Look forward to next week
Tell them you look forward to picking things up with them at the same time next week.
In the case of delayed contacts, remind the person that you have [15 minutes] allocated to them each week, and ask them to prioritize the key things that they want to tell you that week. This will help you to spend your time on the most important elements.

metadata.topic: Annex 2E. Service user reports problems with the exercises or home practice
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2E. Service user reports problems with the exercises or home practice
metadata.module: Annex 2E. Service user reports problems with the exercises or home practice
metadata.section: Annex 2E. Service user reports problems with the exercises or home practice

text:
Annex 2E. Service user reports problems with the exercises or home practice
Service users can report a range of problems with the exercises they were meant to do or with their home practice. Below are some suggestions as to how to respond to some of the most common.

metadata.topic: The person finds the skills too simple, basic or repetitive
metadata.heading_path: The person finds the skills too simple, basic or repetitive
metadata.module: The person finds the skills too simple, basic or repetitive
metadata.section: The person finds the skills too simple, basic or repetitive

text:
The person finds the skills too simple, basic or repetitive
It can help to acknowledge that although the skills may be simple or basic, they are known to be very effective.
Explain the importance of repeated practice to ensure they can use the skills when distressed. It can help to use an analogy.
- "Yes, you're right, these skills in a way are simple. Even though they're simple, they can be quite effective and we need to practise them many times so that we can use them automatically when we are facing a lot of stress.
- Even very simple skills can be very powerful, and they still require a lot of practice. This can help them to become more automatic. For example, in football it is important to practise the same move over and over again so it becomes easier and natural. Even very talented players need to practise. The same is true with the skills in [intervention name]."

metadata.topic: The person says the intervention is making them feel stressed or upset
metadata.heading_path: The person says the intervention is making them feel stressed or upset
metadata.module: The person says the intervention is making them feel stressed or upset
metadata.section: The person says the intervention is making them feel stressed or upset

text:
The person says the intervention is making them feel stressed or upset
Sometimes a breathing exercise can make a person feel dizzy or light-headed. Often, this is because they are breathing too deeply or too quickly. If this happens, remind the person that they should do the exercise in a way that makes them comfortable. Remind them to breathe slowly and gently, or just breathe normally and focus on the other parts of the exercise.
- "This can be a common problem. If you feel dizzy or light-headed most of the time it means you are still learning how to do it well, you may be breathing too quickly or too deeply. Try to breathe more slowly, and focus on noticing the things around you. As you practice, the benefits will become clear."
Sometimes a person may become upset if the intervention causes them to think about difficult situations. You can reassure them that this is okay, and that these feelings do not stay forever. You can suggest that they continue trying the intervention's exercises as they are aimed at reducing distress, and they tend to get easier with practice.
- "When we talk or think about difficult situations, we can experience distressing thoughts and feelings. This is quite common, and it is important to remember that these feelings do not stay forever - rather, they come and go like the weather. It is okay if you do not want to do an exercise, but you might find that trying these exercises will help how you feel.
- I know facing feelings can be hard. Just know that facing difficult feelings today can help you feel better over time and help you reach your goals."
If the intervention is making them feel worse, or a difficulty keeps occurring, discuss this with your supervisor.

metadata.topic: The person did not remember to practise
metadata.heading_path: The person did not remember to practise
metadata.module: The person did not remember to practise
metadata.section: The person did not remember to practise

text:
The person did not remember to practise
Make context-appropriate suggestions, such as setting an alarm or mobile phone reminder, asking someone to remind them, writing a reminder somewhere obvious, or linking it to a predictable daily task, such as washing or dressing in the morning or when arriving home.
- "That's a common problem. It can be hard to remember when we have so many other things going on, but it is really important because it's through practice that we really see the difference. Do you have any ideas on how you could help yourself remember?" [Prompts: set a reminder on your phone, or put a note somewhere in your home.]

metadata.topic: The person says they struggle to do the skills in stressful situations
metadata.heading_path: The person says they struggle to do the skills in stressful situations
metadata.module: The person says they struggle to do the skills in stressful situations
metadata.section: The person says they struggle to do the skills in stressful situations

text:
The person says they struggle to do the skills in stressful situations
Encourage them to first practise during less stressful situations. You could use an analogy to explain this, for example, how a team practises before a football match, or how some people practise cooking a dish for themselves before making it for other people.
- "It is harder to practise in stressful situations, so I'd always recommend practising a lot in less stressful situations to start with - like practising sport with your team before a match, or practising cooking a dish before making it for other people."

metadata.topic: The person says they felt too bad to do the exercises
metadata.heading_path: The person says they felt too bad to do the exercises
metadata.module: The person says they felt too bad to do the exercises
metadata.section: The person says they felt too bad to do the exercises

text:
The person says they felt too bad to do the exercises
Remind them of the rationale for the exercise.
Explain that difficult feelings can occur, but practising the skill should help them with these feelings, so it can be useful to do the exercise even if they do not feel like it.
- "It can be hard to motivate ourselves when we feel low or anxious, but these skills are to help you with these emotions, so they can be useful to do even when you don't feel like it. It's through doing these things, even when we feel bad, that we start to notice a difference in how we feel."
If they have practised the exercises, always praise their efforts, however small, and discuss ways to make practising easier to manage.
- "It's great that you're taking part in [intervention name]. Sometimes people struggle to do the home practice, but you're talking to me about it so that's a really good start. There can be many reasons why practising is hard, let's troubleshoot that together - tell me a bit more about why you are struggling to practise the exercises."

metadata.topic: The person found the skill did not help so is reluctant to try again
metadata.heading_path: The person found the skill did not help so is reluctant to try again
metadata.module: The person found the skill did not help so is reluctant to try again
metadata.section: The person found the skill did not help so is reluctant to try again

text:
The person found the skill did not help so is reluctant to try again
Explain that it can take time before they start to feel better and encourage them to keep trying.
- "It can take a while before people start feeling better using these techniques. I'd encourage you to keep trying as much as you can. Have you noticed any changes, even if very small?"

metadata.topic: The person says they are confused by the exercise
metadata.heading_path: The person says they are confused by the exercise
metadata.module: The person says they are confused by the exercise
metadata.section: The person says they are confused by the exercise

text:
The person says they are confused by the exercise
Use module-specific content to clarify concepts (see Chapters 5. Information for helpers delivering Step-by-Step and 6. Information for helpers delivering Doing What Matters in Times of Stress (DWM)) and encourage them to keep trying.
- "It is okay if some of the course is unclear to you; these are new concepts. Please just continue to work through [intervention name] and try to practise and see what it is like."

metadata.topic: The person indicates not having enough time for the exercises
metadata.heading_path: The person indicates not having enough time for the exercises
metadata.module: The person indicates not having enough time for the exercises
metadata.section: The person indicates not having enough time for the exercises

text:
The person indicates not having enough time for the exercises
See Annex 2J. Service user indicates not having enough time for the intervention or exercises.

Annex 2F. Service user lacks motivation
If the service user tells you they are not motivated to work through a module or do an exercise, follow the steps below.

metadata.topic: 1. Reassure them and validate their experience
metadata.heading_path: 1. Reassure them and validate their experience
metadata.module: 1. Reassure them and validate their experience
metadata.section: 1. Reassure them and validate their experience

text:
1. Reassure them and validate their experience
Tell the person that it is common to feel this way when in a low mood.
- "I see you are having trouble finding the motivation for [intervention name]. It is very common for us to feel less motivated when we have a low mood. Struggling in life often gets us down and this is a natural reaction to adversity."

2. Encourage them
Remind the person of the strength they have shown in starting the intervention.
- "Remember you've shown strength in starting [intervention name] and this is great!"

3. Explore past coping strategies
Talk through the things that the person has done in the past that helped, for example talking to someone in their support network.
- "Let's try to explore together things you've done in the past to cope. Are there people you could talk to who could help you with this?"

metadata.topic: 4. Explain the link between mood and motivation
metadata.heading_path: 4. Explain the link between mood and motivation
metadata.module: 4. Explain the link between mood and motivation
metadata.section: 4. Explain the link between mood and motivation

text:
4. Explain the link between mood and motivation
Explain that as mood improves, it's likely that the person's motivation will also improve.
- "Remember that as your mood improves, it's likely that your motivation will too."

metadata.topic: Annex 2G. Service user does not respect boundaries
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2G. Service user does not respect boundaries
metadata.module: Annex 2G. Service user does not respect boundaries
metadata.section: Annex 2G. Service user does not respect boundaries

text:
Annex 2G. Service user does not respect boundaries
There are many ways people can react to helpers. They may take out their distress or anger on you, or they may want to be your friend and meet you in real life. Your role as their helper is to support them for [15 minutes] a week. You should not meet outside this time. You are not the person's friend.
Below are some ways service users might not respect boundaries, alongside suggestions on how to deal with them.

metadata.topic: The person is being aggressive or insulting or is asking personal questions
metadata.heading_path: The person is being aggressive or insulting or is asking personal questions
metadata.module: The person is being aggressive or insulting or is asking personal questions
metadata.section: The person is being aggressive or insulting or is asking personal questions

text:
The person is being aggressive or insulting or is asking personal questions
Stay kind and empathetic.
- "It sounds like you are feeling quite [frustrated/angry/annoyed] today. I can try to help you as best as I can in the time we have, but to do that it will help if we can talk to each other a bit more calmly. Is it okay for us to continue like that?"
Give a warning about their behaviour.
- "I'm sorry, that type of language is unacceptable and we expect people not to speak to us in this way. I understand you might be distressed and we can only continue if you stop being [rude/ insulting]. Would that be possible? If not, we can stop for this week and start again next time."
Remind them of your role and boundaries.
- "I notice that you want to learn a bit more about me. As we're limited on time, I'm keen to focus on [intervention name] and we have a policy not to answer personal questions about ourselves. My role is to help and support you so let's focus on how you did this week."
If their behaviour continues speak to your supervisor.

metadata.topic: The person contacts you excessively outside your allocated contact times
metadata.heading_path: The person contacts you excessively outside your allocated contact times
metadata.module: The person contacts you excessively outside your allocated contact times
metadata.section: The person contacts you excessively outside your allocated contact times

text:
The person contacts you excessively outside your allocated contact times
Tell them that you are not able to talk at the moment.
- "Unfortunately I'm not able to talk at the moment."
Remind them that you are can only offer limited support about the intervention each week and that you will contact them soon to do a support module.
- "Let's chat at our next support contact. Remember I have [15 minutes] a week and can offer you support about [intervention name]. I look forward to talking with you then."
If it keeps happening, ask your supervisor for advice.

metadata.topic: Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention
metadata.module: Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention
metadata.section: Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention

text:
Annex 2H. A friend or family member calls to ask about the intervention
A service user's partner or family member might call you to ask you who you are and what the service user is doing or sharing with you, or to ask about the intervention. Follow the steps below if this happens.
Throughout these steps, it is important to maintain confidentiality. To prevent a service user's friends or family calling you, do not respond to any calls that come from an unrecognized number. [Add in any intervention-specific information, for example, all numbers for service users should be registered on your helper phones upon assignment.]

metadata.topic: 2. Do not give out any information about the service user
metadata.heading_path: 2. Do not give out any information about the service user
metadata.module: 2. Do not give out any information about the service user
metadata.section: 2. Do not give out any information about the service user

text:
2. Do not give out any information about the service user
Inform the person calling that this is a health programme and that its regulations and confidentiality rules do not allow you to give any information about the service user.
- "I work for a health programme, the confidentiality regulations mean that I cannot give you any information. I don't have the information you're looking for but I can refer you to my supervisor."

metadata.topic: Annex 2I. Service user (or a family member) wants to stop the intervention
metadata.heading_path: Annex 2I. Service user (or a family member) wants to stop the intervention
metadata.module: Annex 2I. Service user (or a family member) wants to stop the intervention
metadata.section: Annex 2I. Service user (or a family member) wants to stop the intervention

metadata.topic: If the service user wants to stop
metadata.heading_path: If the service user wants to stop
metadata.module: If the service user wants to stop
metadata.section: If the service user wants to stop

text:
If the service user wants to stop
Tell them it is okay to want to stop and try to understand more while not putting pressure on them.
- "I understand you want to stop and that's okay. I just want to understand better - what is it that you're unhappy about?"
Choose your response depending on their reason for wanting to stop (see other subsections of Annex 2. Troubleshooting templates). If they still want to stop the modules after you have talked to them, then accept their decision.

metadata.topic: If a family member wants the service user to stop
metadata.heading_path: If a family member wants the service user to stop
metadata.module: If a family member wants the service user to stop
metadata.section: If a family member wants the service user to stop

text:
If a family member wants the service user to stop
Try to get a little more information. If there is a risk issue, discuss it with your supervisor. The person can always stop the intervention and seek support from a local health service.
If the person is happy for you to talk to the family member, contact them to introduce yourself and explain what the intervention is. Always discuss this with your supervisor and never disclose any personal information about the service user.
- "Hi, my name is [your name] and I work for [service name]. I am working with [service user name] and wanted to tell you a bit more about [intervention name] and how it can help."
If the person does not want you to talk to the family member, ask whether there is anything they could say themselves to explain to or show the family member what the intervention is about.
- "Sometimes people might want you to stop doing [intervention name] because they don't understand what it is about. Is there anything that you could tell them or show them that might help them understand what [intervention name] is and how it might help you?"
Reinforce the intervention's benefits and explore what they have found useful so far. Offer encouragement but also recognize they are free to stop if they wish.
- "Has anything from [intervention name], no matter how small, been useful for you? Would you be willing to practise this skill and see if anything else becomes useful in later modules?
- [Intervention name] can be difficult at first, but many people find it useful to stay with it for the full [X] modules. If you don't want to, you're free to stop any time."

Annex 2J. Service user indicates not having enough time for the intervention or exercises

- Help them to identify a time (for example, five minutes) in their week where they can go through the intervention or practise regularly - for example in the evening before going to sleep.
- Remind them they can access the intervention whenever they want.
- Encourage them to start by practising a short exercise from the intervention (such as a breathing or grounding exercise - see Annexes 6. Script for grounding exercise and 7. Script for slow breathing exercise).
- Remind them they can practise these short exercises during other activities, such as waiting in line for something or before going to sleep.
- "It can be hard to get time to ourselves sometimes. The great thing about this intervention is that the modules will not take too long and can make quite a difference.
- Are there times of day or places where interruptions are less likely, and you have some time to yourself? [Prompts: Could you practice when you're doing another activity, such as waiting in line or just before you go to sleep?] Let's try and identify a time each day where you can find five minutes or even just two minutes to practise one of the techniques.

Source: Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions (EASE): group psychological help for young adolescents affected by distress in communities exposed to adversity. Geneva: World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF); 2023. Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO.
Helpers should follow their organization's procedures for assessing imminent risk of suicide. The example protocol below can also be adapted by organizations for their own contexts.
Ask both question 1 and question 2 and record the answers on the form. If the service user has already clearly provided enough information to answer a question, you do not need to ask the question again. First introduce the topic.
Example script for introducing the risk assessment questions:
"I'm glad that you're telling me about this. Sometimes when people are very upset or feel hopeless, they have thoughts about death or ending their own life. These thoughts are not uncommon, and you should not feel ashamed about having such thoughts if you do. I would like to ask you some more questions to better understand how things are for you. Is that okay? Can we continue?"
Question 1: In the past month, have you had thoughts of ending your life or a plan to end your life? Or have you taken any actions to end your life in the past year?
YES
NO
If the answer is "no", circle "no".
If the answer is "yes", ask the person to describe their thoughts, plans or actions taken. Write details here:
Question 2: Are you currently thinking of ending your life, do you have a plan of ending your life, or are you currently taking any steps to end your life?
YES
NO
UNSURE
If the answer is "yes" or the person is "unsure", ask the person to describe their thoughts, plan or actions to you. Write details here:

text:
Annex 3A. Example protocol for assessing imminent risk of suicide
- If the person answers "yes" or "unsure" to Question 2, they may end their life in the near future. Follow the imminent risk steps below.
- If the person answers "yes" to question 1 and "no" or "unsure" to question 2 but is extremely agitated, violent, distressed or not communicating, they may end their life in the near future. Follow the imminent risk steps below.
- If the person answers "yes" to question 1 and "no" to question 2 and they are NOT extremely agitated, violent, distressed or not communicating, they are unlikely to be at imminent risk of self-harm or suicide, but there might still be a risk. You do not need to follow the steps below, but tell the person you will inform your supervisor to discuss any additional support that may be helpful. For example, say this: "It's very important that you have told me how you are feeling. These thoughts can happen when things are really difficult. If at any time you feel this feeling is getting worse, or you feel a risk of harming yourself or ending your life, then please make sure you speak to me." When you talk to the service user, make sure to ask whether they still have thoughts about ending their life and ask question 2 accordingly.
- If the person answers "no" to both question 1 and question 2, thank them for answering your questions and continue with the remainder of the pre-intervention assessment.
- In case of any doubt about a person's safety, talk to your supervisor.

metadata.topic: Imminent risk: Steps to immediately take if the person may end their life in the near future:
metadata.heading_path: Imminent risk: Steps to immediately take if the person may end their life in the near future:
metadata.module: Imminent risk: Steps to immediately take if the person may end their life in the near future:
metadata.section: Imminent risk: Steps to immediately take if the person may end their life in the near future:

text:
Imminent risk: Steps to immediately take if the person may end their life in the near future:
- You must always contact your supervisor immediately. Explain this to the person. For example:
"From what you have described to me, I am concerned about your safety. As I mentioned before, if I believe that you are at risk of ending your life, I must contact my supervisor. This is very important, so we can get you the best kind of help for these problems as soon as possible. I am going to do this now, okay?"
- Ask the person to stay with you online or on the phone.
- Contact someone the person trusts. To find out this information, you could say: "I would also like to contact someone in your community to ensure that you can be kept safe. Who would that be?"
- Ask the person where they could go that will be a place of safety. This could be a hospital, or perhaps to the home of a trusted friend or family member.
- Use your basic helping skills to give the person support while you wait for instructions from your supervisor.
- Ask the person if they have access to any means of self-harm. Discuss ways to remove these items from their home environment.
- Attend to the person's mental state and emotional distress.
- Explore reasons and ways to stay alive.
- Focus on the person's strengths by encouraging them to talk about how earlier problems have been resolved.
- Give them the details of the local services and advise them that they can also contact emergency services if needed.

Ask direct, clear questions
- When asking questions about suicide, avoid using indirect words that could be misunderstood.
- Direct questions help the person feel that they are not being judged for having thoughts or plans of suicide or for having made suicide attempts or self-harmed in the past.
- Some people may feel uncomfortable talking with you about suicide, but you can tell them that it is very important for you to clearly understand their level of safety.
- Asking questions about suicide will not cause the person to take action to end their life, but often helps them feel understood and less distressed.

In the first support contact:
- Try reconnecting with them and remind them that it is important for you to ensure their safety. Check whether they want to continue with the support contact.
- If they do not answer and you are concerned for their safety, you may need to speak with the safety contact agreed at the start of the programme, if there is one.
- Tell the person about different support services available.
- Contact your supervisor to let them know so they can support you.
For information on how to ask questions about suicide and self-harm, and what to do if you are working online and get disconnected while concerned about a person's safety, see section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns?.

Annex 3B. Steps to follow in cases of sexual violence, intimate partner violence or other protection concerns
Sources. Adapted from:
- Group Problem Management Plus (Group PM+): group psychological help for adults impaired by distress in communities exposed to adversity. Generic field-trial version 1.0. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2020 (https://iris.who.int/ handle/10665/334055, accessed 18 September 2025).
- Self-Help Plus (SH+): a group-based stress management course for adults. Generic field-trial version 1.0. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/345349, accessed 18 September 2025).
Remember that people may find it hard to talk about sexual violence or intimate partner violence because of cultural taboos, shame or fear of stigma, or because they may be scared for their safety, or because thinking about their experiences causes them distress. They may face discrimination and rejection from their family, community or wider society. They may be pressured to stay quiet, may be blamed or may not be believed.
If someone chooses to talk about these experiences with you, they are showing great courage and trust. It is very important to show willingness and openness to hearing what they want to share with you.
If you know or suspect that a service user may have experienced or be at immediate risk of intimate partner violence or sexual violence, follow your organization's procedures for responding to safety issues (see section 4.8 How do I manage imminent risk of suicide and other immediate safety concerns?), in addition to following the steps above.
Steps to follow are outlined below.

1. Restate confidentiality
If someone wants to disclose information related to sexual violence or intimate partner violence, it is important to remind them that you will not share what they are telling you with anyone outside the intervention team, unless there are any immediate safety issues that may need to be addressed (see section 3.2.2 Maintain confidentiality).

2. Show empathy and validate the person's story and experience
You can say something like:
- "That sounds like a very difficult and upsetting situation. You have shown a lot of strength in telling me this."

3. Listen without judgement
Give the person space and time to speak. Sometimes people just want someone to listen to their story.
In other cases, they may want or need additional help.

4. If appropriate, point to support organizations
Consider telling the person about any organizations in the area that might be able to help them.
If the person declines help, you can tell them that they can ask for a referral to an organization later. You might say:
- "It can be very difficult going through experiences such as the one you have described. There might be some organizations that can offer further support. Would you like more information about them?"
For more information on addressing sexual violence and intimate partner violence see:
- Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2014 (https://apps.who.int/iris/ handle/10665/136101, accessed 18 September 2025).
- World Health Organization, United Nations Population Fund and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. Clinical management of rape and intimate partner violence survivors: developing protocols for use in humanitarian settings. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2020 (https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/331535, accessed 18 September 2025).
- How to support survivors of gender-based violence when a GBV actor is not available in your area: a step-by-step pocket guide from humanitarian practitioners (version 2.0). Geneva: Inter-Agency Standing Committee; 2015 (https://gbvguidelines.org/en/ documents/pocket-guide-supporting-survivors-for-non-gbv-specialists/, accessed 18 September 2025).

Templates to support supervision include supervision forms for helpers to fill out before their supervision meeting to ensure all important issues are covered (see Annex 4A. Fidelity checklist).

text:
This script is for live contacts.
If a service user is highly distressed, helpers may consider using a grounding exercise to help calm them and bring their distress back to a manageable level.
Below you will find a script for supporting people through a grounding exercise. For highly distressed individuals, it is generally better for them to keep their eyes open during the exercise and to spend the most time on step 3, where they observe things in the external environment, rather than focusing on internal feelings.
Encourage the person to share out loud what they observe in the environment around them. At the end of the exercise, check how they are feeling, and offer to repeat the exercise if they want to.

1. Introduction
- "Remember, there are three steps to grounding. You can keep your eyes open as we go through them. First, notice how you are feeling and what you are thinking right now. Are you feeling stressed or caught in an emotional storm?"

2. Slow down and connect
- "For step 2, slow down and connect with your body. Push your feet into the floor, stretch, and focus on your breathing."

3. Refocus
- "Now for Step 3, we will refocus on the world around us.
- What are five things you can see? [Pause and wait for their response, prompting if needed.]
- What are three or four things you can hear? [Pause and wait for their response, prompting if needed.]
- Reach out and touch something - like whatever you are sitting on. What does it feel like under your fingers? [Pause and wait for their response, prompting if needed.]
- Notice where you are and what you are doing." [Prompt them to say aloud where they are and what they are doing.]

4. Check in
- "We just did a brief grounding exercise together. How are you feeling?"

5. Repeat if necessary
- "Is this something that you feel able to do yourself, or would you like to repeat the exercise together now?"

text:
This script is for live contacts.
If a service user is highly distressed, helpers may consider using a slow breathing exercise to help calm them and bring their distress back to a manageable level.
Below you will find a script for supporting people through a slow breathing exercise. At the end of the exercise, check how they are feeling, and offer to repeat the exercise if they want to.

1. Introduction
- "I'm going to guide you through a slow breathing exercise. I'll read the instructions and at times I'll stop talking so you have time to practise.
- The idea is that when we are stressed, we often take shorter, quick little breaths. This can make us feel even more tense. We can use this exercise to slow down our breathing to help us reduce the stress and tension.
[pause 1 second]
- Before we start, I want you to relax your body a bit.
- Shake out your arms and legs, and let them go floppy and loose. Take a few seconds to do that now." [pause 5 seconds]

2. Get comfortable
- "Great, now try to sit in a comfortable position with your back straight. Roll your shoulders back and gently move your head from side to side."
[pause 5 seconds]

3. Begin
- "Okay, we're ready to begin.
[pause 1 second]
- We are going to start by breathing in through the nose and out through the mouth. [pause 1 second]
- Take a few breaths now, in through your nose and out through your mouth. You don't have to make an effort, just breathe normally and focus on exhaling." [pause 10 seconds]
- "That's great, now just take a few more." [pause 5 seconds]

4. Slow breathing down
- "Okay good. Now the next step is to slow your breathing down. Try to take around three seconds to breathe in through your nose and three seconds to breathe out through your mouth. I will count for you.
- So breathe in, one [1 second], two [1 second], three [1 second].
- And breathe out, one [1 second], two [1 second], three [1 second].
- And again, breathe in, [1 second], two [1 second], three [1 second].
- And breathe out, one [1 second], two [1 second], three [1 second]."

5. Repeat
- "Do you notice how slowly I counted? That is about how long it can take for you to take a slow breath in and out.
- We will now repeat this exercise for about half a minute and I will count the breaths for us." [repeat, counting breaths for about 30 seconds]

6. Check in
- "How was that for you? [pause 2 seconds]
- Take a few moments to just notice how your body feels. Has there been any change? Do you feel less tense?
[pause 5 seconds]
- If not, that is okay, sometimes it takes a little practice. I would encourage you to practise because over time, this technique could help.
- Remember that the aim is to help reduce your stress, so if you find yourself becoming more stressed from doing this, or worrying about doing it right, then just do whatever feels good and does not cause you stress.
[pause 1 second]
- Is this something that you feel able to do yourself, or would you like to repeat the exercise together now?"
